report.title: Running the cell logic on FPGA or custom hardware: per-event inventory, precision tests, a PE design, and time semantics (hw/mapping)
report.summary: Yes, the cell logic maps well onto custom hardware, but not in its current bit-exact float64 form. The bitwise contract requires every float64 operation in a fixed left-to-right order plus exp/log/tanh identical to glibc's. AMD's floating-point cores are only 1-ULP accurate for exp and log, so a bit-exact FPGA port would be large, slow per element, and no better than CPUs. Behaviour does not need that precision. I tested 79 arithmetic variants on 3 evolved bodies with 512–1,024 paired lives each. Storing cell state in float32 changed nothing in 99–100% of lives. A combined fixed-point profile ("hw12": 12-bit genes and morphogens, 8 fractional bits on weights, accumulators and traces, events on a 1/256 time grid) moved F by only −0.9% to +2.1%, within noise. Even a 1/64 grid was harmless; 1/16 cost 2–4% and coarser grids 4–12%. The model is also already shaped for parallel hardware: every cross-site effect is delayed by at least d_min = 0.5. So a processor array that pauses at a barrier every 0.5 model units gives bitwise the same lives as the production kernel; I checked this on 288 life comparisons. That barrier is only a progress fence, not a clock inside the model. My PE sketches are estimates, not built. A fixed-point design with time-shared processing elements on one AWS F2 FPGA (VU47P) might reach roughly 2,000–7,000 lives/s, about 1–4 rented 192-core CPU boxes. That is perhaps 5–20× cheaper per unit of work, but it takes about 6–12 person-months of FPGA work and a new integer version of the model. Since a whole 29-run pilot already costs only $6–16 on CPUs, the case for hardware is your long-term "cells in silicon" goal and per-life latency (about 4 ms per life on a one-processor-per-site array, against 70–150 ms on a CPU core), not evolution throughput. The practical next step is to write the integer "twin" of the model that the ABI already reserves (flag bit 10, LIFE_ABI.md section 13), using the measured widths.

findings.claim: Per-event inventory: the TICK handler does about 95% of all arithmetic. One GRN tick in the C kernel costs about 670 multiplies, 674 adds, 39 divides, 15 exp, 2 tanh, 35 rint and 6 splitmix64 calls, and sends about 5.6 morphogen packets. Per tick: readout + decode + derive about 860 mul+add, the GRN about 432, chemistry 24, inbox 11, membrane re-anchor 5. Other handlers per event: FIRE + broadcast 27 mul, 1.4 exp, 28.5 splitmix (one jitter draw per live neighbour), 5.7 messages. Membrane step (ARRIVAL/RECEPTOR) about 6 mul, 10 add, 3 div, 2 exp. Receptor candidate (RCAND) 1 log + 4 splitmix. Accountant thinning per RCAND 14 mul, 2 exp, 14 splitmix. BORN/PRESENT/ACK notice 17 splitmix + 1 exp (contact-delay normal). BIRTH about 443 mul, 28 splitmix, 8 messages. CLAIM resolve: compares only.

findings.claim:
Structural sparsity makes the hardware tick much cheaper than the kernel's dense loops.
- Every evolved genome has exactly 8 active genes.
- About 136 of the 200 active-row GRN weights are nonzero (the inactive gene columns are zero).
- Every lambda is a power of 2 (1/64 to 1/2), so g += lambda(s-g) is a shift and an add.
- tau_tr is in {2,4,8,16} and n_view/D = n/8, so those divisions are shifts. Only m/(1+m) needs a reciprocal (a lookup table).
- A sparse tick therefore needs about 380 MACs (136 GRN + 184 readout + about 60 derive/chemistry) instead of the kernel's 768 dense.

findings.claim:
The bitwise float64 contract is far stricter than the behaviour needs.
- Bitwise equality needs every float64 operation unfused and in source order, plus glibc-identical exp/log/tanh/sin/cos/pow. FPGA vendor exp/log cores are only 1-ULP accurate, so they cannot match glibc.
- Yet rounding all cell-side state to binary32 left F unchanged (to 1e-6) in 99-100% of lives, and rounding exp/log results to 24 significant bits left it unchanged in 100%.
- The model's own grids (the Q10 membrane, the 1/8-grid knobs, the rint table decodes) absorb small errors.

findings.claim:
Which single quantisations are harmless (all 3 bodies within 2 paired SE, or under 0.2%, and under 5%), and which are not:
- Gene state g in [0,1]: needs at least 10 fractional bits; 8 bits costs 6.7% on speck_s5. Cause: slow genes (lambda 1/64) freeze when lambda*|s-g| is below half an LSB, as ONE_LIFE_DESIGN.md already noted.
- Sigmoid output: 6 bits.
- GRN pre-activation and readout accumulators: 3-6 fractional bits.
- Weights W, b, A, a0, Q: 4 fractional bits; W needs sign + 5 integer bits.
- Morphogens m, amt, conc: 6 fractional bits, 3 integer bits.
- Traces f, r, rho: even 2 fractional bits are harmless.
- Twitch z: 6 bits; at 4 bits the click key (thresholds 0.6/0.25) shifts and lmax4_s5 loses 8.4%.
- Cell-side exp/log results: 6 significant bits.
- GRN inputs x[16..22]: 8 bits.

findings.claim:
Event-time grid (a synchronous FPGA with quantised event times).
- A grid of 2^-6 unit (d_min/32) or finer is harmless. 2^-5 and 2^-4 cost about 2-4%. 2^-3 costs 4-7% and 2^-2 costs about 12%.
- Coarse grids exercise the tie rules that are measure-zero in the exact model: same-site coincidences become frequent and claim ties appear.
- Both are resolved deterministically by the existing ABI rules: the batch order (claims < notices < packets < membrane <\ tick) and the lowest daughter uid.

findings.claim: A PE array with a global barrier every h <= d_min of model time reproduces the production kernel bitwise. The ABI's window scheduler is exactly that schedule: every site processes its own events of the window independently and in any order. This holds because every cross-site message, including the world's RECEPTOR, is delayed by at least d_min = 0.5. Parallelism per 0.5-unit window is about 32-61 active sites per body, with at most 11-12 events at one site in one window.

findings.claim:
PE sketch, fixed-point, one lattice site. All figures are estimates and nothing was synthesised.
- Datapath: 1-4 DSP48E2 MACs (16-bit g and inputs x 12-18-bit weights, 48-bit accumulators); one BRAM18 of function tables (sigmoid, exp(-x), -log(u), tanh, 1/(1+m)); a small compare/clip/rint unit for decode; shift-add gene update.
- Event front-end: 8 link FIFOs plus 3 self timers (TICK, THRESHOLD, RCAND), and a minimum-timestamp selector that forms same-time batches in ABI group order.
- Genome: one BRAM18 copy per PE, or a ROM shared by a PE cluster. Hash: a pipelined splitmix64 unit shared by about 16 PEs.
- Timing: about 449 cycles per tick with 1 DSP, 164 with 4 (sparse 380 MACs); spike arrival about 12 cycles; fire about 22 cycles + 1 flit per neighbour; receptor candidate about 10; packet receive 2.
- Link messages: ARRIVAL = 1 flit (time 32, target tag 16, 2-bit channel mask). PACKET = 2 flits (amt and conc at 4 x 16). CLAIM = about 6 flits (two uids + 16 daughter genes x 12). Load is about 6 flits per model unit per PE, about 1-2% of a 64-bit link.
- Division: the mother scores the open slots, partitions g and sends a CLAIM. The empty target PE (always listening) arbitrates in its batch, rebuilds its frozen physics from hash(seed, sitekey, k), runs readout/decode, sends BORN to its neighbours and ACK through bslot. No allocator is needed.
- Death: alive = 0, DIED to the neighbours; stale events are dropped by uid/version tags.

findings.claim:
Time and clocklessness:
(a) A synchronous FPGA with a barrier every h <= d_min keeps the model clockless. The FPGA clock and the barrier never enter the model: event times are data, and the d_min lookahead makes the result independent of the order in which PEs finish (verified bitwise). Quantising event times is optional; it is needed only for bucketed event queues, and its effects are measured above.
(b1) Asynchronous circuits (QDI or bundled-data) or GALS, with timestamps carried as data and local promises (Chandy-Misra-Bryant: 'nothing from me before t + d_min'), are exact and use no global barrier or clock. This is the most faithful clockless implementation.
(b2) Asynchronous circuits that turn model delays into physical delays lose determinism:
- claim ties are resolved by arbiters (first arrival, possibly metastable)
- left-limit reads become races, and the within-instant batch order is undefined
- jitter becomes physical, so hash-keyed frozen physics and common random numbers are lost
- there is no bitwise reference, so evolution would need hardware in the loop
(c) Neuromorphic chips such as Loihi run asynchronous circuits but discrete algorithmic time steps with barrier synchronisation. The cell model then becomes time-stepped, and GRN, decode, division and death would need microcode or embedded cores and pre-allocated neurons.

options.option: A. Bit-exact float64 port to FPGA (keep ABI 3)
options.speedup_or_benefit: Probably none, and likely slower per dollar than CPUs. [E] A float64 PE (a shared IEEE multiply-add unit, a divider, and exp/log/tanh rebuilt to match glibc's algorithms bit for bit) needs about 8-15k LUTs and about 15 DSPs, so about 60-110 PEs per VU47P. Each PE takes about 10 us per tick because the left-to-right sums form dependent chains, against 1.9 us per tick on a laptop E-core. That gives roughly 20-50 E-core equivalents per FPGA.
options.semantic_changes: None if done perfectly: bitwise equal to kernel.c and reference.py.
options.effort: 12-24 person-months [E], mostly reproducing glibc 2.39's FMA-path exp/log/tanh/pow/sin/cos in RTL and verifying them bit for bit; expert FPGA and floating-point skills.
options.cost: F2 $1.98/h on-demand, $0.659/h spot [S]. Engineering dominates.
options.risks: AMD's own exp/log cores are only 1-ULP accurate [S PG060], so custom units are mandatory. Any glibc change breaks equality. Little throughput gain for very large effort.

options.option: B. Integer-twin ABI + virtual-PE FPGA array (throughput design; AWS F2 VU47P, Alveo U55C or V80)
options.speedup_or_benefit: [E] About 3,800 lives/s per VU47P/U55C and about 9,000 per V80 for speck_s5-size bodies (range about 2-7k on the VU47P given ±2x on LUTs per PE and utilisation). That is about 570 laptop E-cores, or about 1-4 rented 192-core boxes per FPGA (per wall-hour). Per dollar on F2 on-demand: about 8-21x cheaper per unit of work than the CPU box, or about 5-15x against an integer-twin CPU kernel. A 500-generation run of about 1,070 lives per generation would take about 2.5-5 minutes on one FPGA.
options.semantic_changes: A new arithmetic contract: the integer twin reserved as flag bit 10 in LIFE_ABI.md section 13, with widths from this study (hw12 profile; time grid 2^-8). Lives differ from ABI 3 trajectory by trajectory, but evolved-body F moved only -0.9% to +2.1% [M]. Integer sums are associative, so the inbox sort and the canonical ordering of sums disappear. Bitwise equality between a C reference and the RTL returns by construction. Clocklessness is kept: barrier windows of h <= d_min, verified bitwise.
options.effort: About 1-2 person-months to specify and implement the integer twin in C and the Python reference, with tests; about 6-12 person-months for RTL or Vitis HLS PEs, the event front-end, a per-body world/accountant unit, host integration, and bitwise co-simulation against the C twin [E].
options.cost: F2 f2.6xlarge $1.98/h on-demand or $0.659/h spot [S]. U55C and V80 card prices not verified.
options.risks: Re-evolution under integer arithmetic must be checked: hw10 already costs 2.8% on one body, so stay at hw12 or above. The CATCH world/accountant (receptor thinning about 111k per life, dot dynamics, clicks) must also go into hardware, or the host becomes the bottleneck. Every planned model change must then be made twice (C and RTL). My PE resource numbers are unsynthesised estimates.

options.option: C. Integer twin + spatial PE array, one PE per site (literal 'cells in silicon')
options.speedup_or_benefit: [E] Throughput is poor: about 1 body per VU47P/U55C (region radius 6 x 4 planes = 508 PEs; radius 7 = 676 does not fit) and about 2 per V80, giving about 230-550 lives/s, i.e. 34-82 E-cores. Latency is the benefit: a T=1024 life in about 4 ms against 70-150 ms on a CPU core (20-40x), which suits real-time embodied demos. It is also the direct prototype for the long-term goal.
options.semantic_changes: As B, plus a finite region. fabric_R=7 x 4 planes left 97-100% of lives identical; R=6 changed F by at most 0.2% [M]. Wall rejections are an existing ABI semantic.
options.effort: About 2-4 person-months for a small single-plane radius-3 prototype (37 PEs) on a dev board; about 6-9 for a full region [E].

options.option: D. Integer twin + tick-engine pipelines (maximum throughput)

options.cost: As B.

options.option: E. Clockless asynchronous implementation (QDI/bundled-data ASIC, or GALS FPGA with Chandy-Misra-Bryant local promises)

options.semantic_changes: With timestamps as data and local promises: exact, identical to the integer-twin reference. If model delays become physical delays: nondeterministic arbitration, no bitwise reference, physical jitter instead of hash-keyed frozen physics, and evolution needs hardware in the loop.
options.effort: GALS on an FPGA: about 3-6 person-months on top of C or B [E]. Asynchronous ASIC: multi-year, specialist async-design skills.
options.cost: ASIC shuttles are covered by the platforms study; not priced here.
options.risks: Async tool flows are niche. The world/accountant node is global and must also emit promises. Physical-delay variants cannot reproduce evolved results.

options.option: F. Neuromorphic chips (Loihi 2 / SpiNNaker2-class)
options.speedup_or_benefit: Low fit. Loihi-class chips advance in barrier-synchronised discrete time steps [S]; GRN, decode, division and death are not native neuron operations. SpiNNaker-class would just run the C kernel on ARM cores.
options.semantic_changes: The model becomes time-stepped at the chip's step (a 2^-6 grid or finer is needed to stay within about 1% [M]). Growth needs pre-allocated neurons and reconfiguration.
options.effort: High (microcode plus embedded-core programming); access through research programmes.
options.cost: Not priced (see the platforms study).
options.risks: Intel archived the Lava SDK on 2026-05-13 (platforms study sources.md, unverified by me). Structural plasticity is unsupported.

options.option: G. Integer twin on CPUs first (software only)
options.speedup_or_benefit: [E] About 1.3-1.6x per core from fixed-point tick arithmetic (the throughput study measured 0.25-0.30 us vs 0.50-0.65 us per tick) plus order-free sums; this stacks with the audit's 1.26-1.36x fast mode. It is the prerequisite for B-E and makes results bitwise portable across CPUs, glibc versions and ARM.
options.semantic_changes: As B: a new arithmetic contract with measured small dF (hw12).
options.effort: About 1-2 person-months, Python reference included [E].
options.cost: None beyond CPU time for a confirmation pilot.
options.risks: Needs a short re-evolution pilot to confirm evolvability; the goldens change.

recommendations: Do not build FPGA hardware for evolution throughput now. A 29-run pilot costs $6-16 on rented CPUs; the best FPGA design is estimated at about 1-4 CPU boxes per device and 5-20x cheaper per unit of work, after a model change and about 6-12 person-months.

Specify and implement the reserved integer twin (LIFE_ABI.md section 13, flag bit 10) using this study's widths, not the planned Q24 and 2^-20 time.
- g at least Q12 (Q10 is the floor; Q8 freezes slow genes)
- sigmoid output 12 bits
- weights with 8 fractional bits (W needs sign + 5 integer bits; A sign + 2)
- GRN and readout accumulators with 8 fractional bits
- morphogens Q12 with 3 integer bits
- traces with 8 fractional bits and 7 integer bits
- twitch at least 8 bits
- table-based exp/log with 12 or more significant bits
- event times on a 2^-8 grid (2^-6 also passed)
Use integer sums, so the inbox sort and canonical ordering go away. Keep splitmix64 for draws. Build the C twin, the Python reference and a bitwise test, then run a short re-evolution pilot under it.

Keep the causality contract as a hard design rule for every planned change: every cross-site effect, the world included, delayed by at least d_min, with no zero-delay reads. It is what makes barrier windows, GALS and local-promise hardware exact. With faster conduction (d0 = 0.5) keep d_min at 0.5, or accept proportionally more windows. With the radius gene (radius 2), keep two-hop messages at or above d_min; forwarding latency is then wall time, not model time.

For the long-term goal of cell logic running on hardware, prototype one fixed-point PE (Vitis HLS from the C integer twin is fastest), co-simulate it bitwise against the twin, then build a small spatial array (one plane, radius 3) on a dev board or an F2 instance. Consider a GALS version with Chandy-Misra-Bryant local promises as the clockless variant. Region size: radius 6-7 x 4 planes left these bodies unchanged.

If throughput on hardware is ever needed (100x larger experiments), use the virtual-PE design (B) on AWS F2 (VU47P, $1.98/h on-demand or $0.659/h spot) rather than buying cards. Put the CATCH world/accountant in hardware too: receptor thinning is about 111k operations per life and would otherwise starve the host.

Budget the planned model changes in hardware terms. Gene duplication grows the per-tick MACs as about G(G+9) + 23G (380 at 8 active genes, about 770 at 16). Per-channel face weights add readout rows. The radius gene grows links from 8 to about 20 per PE, or needs two-hop forwarding. A per-region receptor rate (from the audit) would remove most of the 54% of events that are rejected receptor candidates, on CPU and on hardware alike.

verdict.title: Re-check of hw/mapping: the exactness and precision results hold, but FPGA throughput and cost gains are overstated about 2-3x

checks.claim: A processor array with a barrier every h <= d_min (0.5) gives bitwise the same lives as the production heap kernel. Every cross-site effect, including the world's RECEPTOR, is delayed by at least d_min, so the barrier is a progress fence and not a clock inside the model.
checks.recheck: [M] I built my own instrumented copy of the kernel (verify/kernel_v.c, made by verify/patch.py). With all hooks off it is bitwise the production kernel on 16 new lives x 3 bodies (verify/balance_v.jsonl). I ran new seeds, fresh_seeds(16, seed0=37,500,000), in three configurations: h=0.5 with tie/order seeds 0; h=0.5 with tie seed 12345 and order seed 987654321; h=0.25 with seeds 777/31337. Each was compared with the heap run on all 5 hashes and all 57 ledger columns. I also re-read LIFE_ABI.md sections 1, 6.3 and 11.2.
checks.result: 9 of 9 body x configuration combinations were bitwise equal (144 life comparisons), including the runs with non-zero tie and order seeds. So the result does not depend on the order in which sites are visited. ABI 6.3 confirms that RECEPTOR is created by the accountant at t and arrives at t + d_min. Caveat the study under-weights: the window scheduler (marked 'tests only' in the ABI) still runs one sequential accountant per body. It sorts each window's records into canonical order (t, sk, seq) and does the receptor thinning against the dot position just before t. That is a serial stage per body, not a parallel one.

checks.claim: On a spatial array (one 1-DSP processor per site) a T=1024 life takes about 4.4 ms, against 70-150 ms on a CPU core (2.0 ms with 4-DSP processors).
checks.recheck: [M] I instrumented the window loop with the study's own cycle table (tick 449 or 164 cycles, membrane step 12, fire 22 + 1 per neighbour, receptor candidate 10, packet 2, birth, claim, notice). Per window I recorded the cycles of the busiest site, the record count and the receptor-candidate count (verify/window_v.jsonl, 16 new lives per body). [E] I then added an accountant that handles 1 record per cycle plus 1, 4 or 14 cycles per thinning test (verify/recompute.py).
checks.result: Processor side confirmed: the busiest site takes 465-514 cycles per window with 1 DSP and 195-229 with 4 DSPs. That is 0.95-1.05M cycles per life, about 4.0-4.4 ms (1.8-2.0 ms) at 250 MHz. 94-99.7% of windows have a tick in their busiest site. But the accountant is left out. It sees 139-283 records and 33-57 thinning tests per window on average (up to 553 and 119). With h = d_min, the RECEPTORs from window k land in window k+1, so a serial accountant adds 340-1,080 cycles to each window. That gives 7-13 ms per life unless its work overlaps with the processors through fine-grained local lookahead. Halving h to pipeline the accountant does not help: the measured critical path rises to 1.74-1.98M cycles, about 1.9x.

checks.claim: The combined fixed-point profile hw12 moved F by only -0.9% to +2.1%, within noise. Storing cell state in float32 changed nothing in 99-100% of lives.
checks.recheck: [M] I re-ran 1,024 new-seed lives per body (seed0 37,500,000) for exact, hw12, f32 and a stricter variant, hw12abs (exp/log results on an absolute 2^-12 fixed-point grid instead of 12 relative bits). Files: verify/quant_v.py and quant_v.jsonl. I also split the study's own 1,024-life hw12 run into two halves.
checks.result: New seeds, hw12: speck_s5 +1.0 ± 1.2%, speck_s0 -2.1 ± 1.6% (95% CI -5.1 to +1.0), lmax4_s5 +0.0 ± 0.85%. hw12abs: +0.7%, -2.7 ± 1.6%, -0.1%. Pooled with the study's run (2,048 lives per body): +0.05 ± 0.85%, 0.0 ± 1.1% and -0.2 ± 0.6%. So no effect is detectable, and the 95% bound is about ±2%. The halves of the study's speck_s0 run differ (-1.8% vs +5.9%), so single-body estimates scatter by several %. f32: F stayed within 1e-6 in 99.1-99.9% of lives, but the hashes changed in 100% of lives, so 'changed nothing' overstates it. Gaps in the emulation: the transforms that turn random draws into normal or exponential values, the world and accountant (cos, sin, pow, thinning exp), and tau and the frozen physics all stay float64. A real integer twin is therefore untested beyond the cell-side state. Also, lambda can reach 1/128 (spec.decode_lambda). With Q12 such genes freeze whenever |s-g| < 2^-6, so Q14-16 is safer than Q12.

checks.claim: The virtual-PE design reaches about 3,800 lives/s per VU47P (range 2-7k), about 570 laptop E-cores, which is 1-4 rented 192-core boxes per FPGA.
checks.recheck: [M] Cycles per life with the study's 4-DSP cost table: 12.27M (speck_s5), against the study's 11.7M. Load balance per window when a body is spread over 8 processors (site index mod 8): 0.62, 0.54 and 0.59. [S] PicoRV32, a minimal CPU core, takes 761-2,019 LUTs (github.com/YosysHQ/picorv32 README, fetched 2026-10-09). [E] Recomputed with an accountant per resident body (4-8k LUTs), 3-8k LUTs per processor, utilisation 0.45-0.6 and a 200-250 MHz clock (verify/recompute.py).
checks.result: The study's 0.6 utilisation equals the load imbalance alone (0.54-0.62), leaving nothing for barriers, accountant stalls or memory-port conflicts. The accountant (one per resident body, 37 in all) is missing from the LUT budget. 3k LUTs per processor, covering event queues, the decode for 23 knobs, division and death logic and links, is the optimistic end. Block RAM is under-counted (64 sites x 1,521 bits = 5.3 BRAM18, against 4 assumed) but does not bind. The shared hash unit is fine at 0.6 utilisation (0.76 calls per cycle) but saturates at full use (1.27). Corrected, in lives/s: optimistic about 3,100 (470 E-core equivalents); mid about 1,400 (216); pessimistic about 730 (110). At the compute audit's estimate that a server core is 2-2.6x a laptop E-core (estimated, not measured), a 192-core box is 384-499 E-core equivalents. So one F2 FPGA is about 0.2-1.2 boxes, central about 0.5, not 1-4. Even the study's own 550-570 E-core figure is only 1.1-1.5 boxes on that basis.

checks.claim: Cost: one F2 FPGA is about 5-20x (8-21x) cheaper per unit of work than CPUs. A 29-run pilot would take about 0.4 FPGA-hours, about $0.8, against $6-16 on CPUs.

VU47P: 1,303,680 LUTs, 9,024 DSPs, 2,016 BRAM36, 960 URAM (270 Mb), 16 GB HBM, 3 SLRs (3 system monitors). The shell 'provides 250MHz clk_main_a0'. Loihi: 'fixed-size discrete time-step model' and 'barrier synchronization ... flush any spikes in flight'. All confirmed. The note that 'Lava was archived 2026-05-13' was not re-checked; it is not load-bearing.

checks.claim: Structural sparsity: lambda is always a power of 2, every evolved genome has exactly 8 active genes, and a sparse tick needs about 380 MACs against 768 dense.
checks.recheck: I read spec.decode_lambda and G_INIT in src/life/spec.py and recomputed the MAC formula G(G+9) + 23G + 60.
checks.result: lambda = 2^-(1+clip(rint(x+3),0,6)) is a power of 2 by construction (1/2 to 1/128), so the gene update is a shift and an add. The 8 active genes equal G_INIT = 8, the number of active slots at initialisation. It is not a structural limit: gene duplication or activation would change it (380 MACs at G=8, about 770 at G=16). The arithmetic of 136 + 184 + 60 = 380 is correct.

verdict.corrected_summary:
Yes, the local cell logic can run on custom hardware, and the study's three main technical results hold up.

1. A bit-exact float64 FPGA port is pointless. AMD's exp/log cores are accurate to 1 ULP, so a port would have to rebuild glibc's algorithms in hardware.
2. A fixed-point "integer twin" at hw12 widths has no detectable effect on F. I replicated this on new seeds; pooled over 2,048 lives per body, the change is within about ±2% (95%). Two corrections to the widths: keep g at Q14-16 if genes with lambda 1/128 appear, and the world, the random-draw transforms and the time arithmetic are still untested in fixed point.
3. A barrier every h <= d_min = 0.5 is bitwise exact. I re-verified this with different tie and order seeds. The model stays clockless, because the barrier and the hardware clock never enter model time.

The performance and cost numbers are optimistic.
- **Throughput.** A virtual-processor design on one AWS F2 FPGA (VU47P) reaches about 700-3,100 lives/s, central about 1,400. The study said about 3,800 (range 2-7k). That is about 110-470 laptop E-cores, or about 0.2-1.2 rented 192-core boxes (central about 0.5), not 1-4 boxes.
- **Why lower.** The per-body accountant/world is a serial unit the study left out. Measured load imbalance alone uses up the 0.6 utilisation it assumed. The 3k LUTs per processor is the optimistic end.
- **Cost.** Like for like, the FPGA is about 1-6x cheaper per unit of work (central 2-3x, about 1.5-2x against an integer-twin CPU kernel), not 5-20x. A 29-run pilot would cost $1-4 on F2 against $6-16 on CPUs.
- **Spatial array (one processor per site).** About 4-13 ms per life rather than 4 ms, because the serial accountant must keep up with every 0.5-unit window. Only one body fits per VU47P, and only if each processor stays under about 1.8k LUTs. Even so it is 5-35x lower latency than a 70-150 ms laptop core.

The recommendation stands, and more strongly:
- Do not build FPGA hardware for evolution throughput.
- Build the integer twin first, in C and the Python reference, and emulate the whole datapath (draws, world, accountant) before fixing the widths.
- Keep the d_min causality rule.
- Prototype hardware only for the long-term cells-in-silicon goal: one processor, then a small array, designing the accountant/world into the array from the start.

Effort is likely above the 6-12 person-months estimate for someone who is not an FPGA specialist, and every planned model change would have to be built twice (C and hardware).
verdict.missed:
1. **The accountant/world is the hidden central bottleneck.** It handles 139-283 records and 33-57 receptor thinnings per 0.5-unit window, in canonical order, against the dot state just before each event. It is left out of the LUT budget, the lives/s figure and the latency figure. In a cells-in-silicon design it is the one global, sequential part.
2. **Lowering d_min costs latency on the spatial array.** 94-99.7% of windows have a tick on their critical path, so halving the window nearly doubles life latency (measured 1.9x). This matters for the planned d0 = 0.5 and radius-gene changes if d_min ever drops below 0.5.
3. **The host could become the bottleneck.** Python per generation (0.2-0.4% of 175 CPU-s, about 0.35-0.7 s) is about as long as one FPGA generation at the corrected rates (about 0.35-1.5 s). Runs would have to be overlapped, or the host halves throughput.
4. **The latency argument for real-time demos is weak.** One body already runs T=1024 in 0.07-0.15 s on a laptop core, faster than real time unless a model unit is mapped to well under a millisecond.
5. **A batched GPU or SIMD option for the integer twin was not considered.** The window formulation that makes FPGA arrays exact also allows batched SIMD/GPU tick processing across lives; ticks are about 78% of processor cycles. The earlier "GPU unhelpful" verdict was for the exact heap kernel only.
6. **Minor points.**
   - The study's quant_table printed only the last run per variant, so its 512-life hw12 run (-1.65/-1.8/-0.8%) is not shown. Its speck_s0 halves differ by 7.7 points, so the per-body numbers are noisier than the single figures suggest.
   - "f32 changed nothing" ignores that the hashes changed in every life.
   - The 8 active genes are the starting count (G_INIT), not a fixed property.
   - The 250 MHz is the AWS shell's interface clock; a design spread over 3 SLRs at about 70% LUT use may not reach it.
   - The person-month estimates assume an FPGA expert, and every planned model change must be made in both C and hardware.

report.title: Running cell-dev cells on FPGAs, neuromorphic chips, GPUs and custom silicon: a platform survey (2026-10-09)
report.summary: Yes, custom hardware could run the model faster, but none of it can run the current exact kernel. That kernel is event-driven, uses float64 and libm, and must match the reference bit for bit. Every faster platform needs a new hardware version of the model (an "ABI") that uses fixed-point numbers and integer timestamps, or one that advances in fixed time steps. For evolution throughput today, it would not pay off. A pilot costs about 217 laptop-CPU-hours, which is $2-16 of rented CPU, so even a 5-70x cheaper FPGA would save only about $1.4-2.4 per pilot against an estimated 4-9 person-months of engineering. My estimates: a fixed-point, event-driven FPGA design that carries event times as data would give about 350-4,200 laptop-core equivalents per F2 FPGA. A time-stepped GPU version would give about 55-2,400 per RTX 4090 at dt=1/16, and only 14-590 at dt=1/64. The GPU version brings a model clock: I measured that at dt=1/16, 3-5% of spikes share a time bin with a spike from a lattice neighbour, and at dt=1/64 about 1% do. Among neuromorphic chips, SpiNNaker2 matches the model's semantics best: programmable ARM cores, local multicast messages and asynchronous execution between cores. Loihi 2 is now risky because Intel archived Lava on 2026-05-13. BrainScaleS-2 runs analog neurons 1000x faster than biology and has already done in-the-loop evolution of an embodied agent, but each chip holds only 512 neurons and results are not exactly reproducible. SynSense, TrueNorth and NorthPole do not fit. For the long-term goal of cells as circuits, a 250 MHz FPGA clock is only an implementation detail when event times are carried as data, as a CPU's clock is today. A truly clockless tissue would be a tile-per-cell chip where each tile runs on its own oscillator, which maps onto each cell's jittered tick. Prototyping such a chip is now cheap (Tiny Tapeout EUR 70 per tile, wafer.space $2-8k for 1,000 dies, chipIgnite $14,950). In such a chip, storing the genome in every cell, not the logic, takes most of the area. Speed is not the obstacle for embodiment: one laptop core already runs a 100-cell body 9-15x faster than real time if one model unit is 1 ms.

findings.claim: Compute is too cheap today for hardware acceleration to pay off on evolution throughput. The case for hardware is embodiment, energy and the clockless substrate, not dollars per run.
findings.evidence: MEASURED/SOURCED in results/catch_pilot/compute_audit.json (prices observed 2026-10-09): spot CPU costs $0.0085-0.0111 per laptop-CPU-hour (L-h), and a pilot is about 217 L-h, $6-16 on one c8a.48xlarge. ESTIMATED (hw_estimates.py): even the optimistic fixed-point FPGA design saves only $1.4-2.4 per pilot. Engineering is 4-9 person-months, about $40k-180k assuming $10-20k per person-month, so break-even is tens of thousands of pilots. Even a 100x larger study (about 22,000 L-h) costs about $200-250 on spot CPUs.

findings.claim: No platform can run the current exact kernel faster in a useful way, because the bitwise float64/libm contract blocks it. Every real speedup needs a new hardware ABI (integer time, fixed-point state, lookup-table exp/sigmoid, a cheap counter-based RNG), or a time-stepped approximation.
findings.evidence: Spec (src/life/spec.py, kernel.c): float64 with glibc exp/log/tanh, about 1.18M exp per speck_s5 life (audit). The audit also notes that glibc picks FMA variants at load time, so even the CPU reference depends on the machine. ESTIMATED: matching glibc bit for bit in FPGA double-precision logic is possible but costs many DSPs and gains little. A fixed-point redesign is roughly 5-10x denser.

findings.claim: Measured hardware-relevant statistics of 4 evolved pilot bests (12 lives each, T=1024; seeds fresh_seeds(12, seed0=37,100,000) because the task's seed template was broken, so index 1 was assumed). Bodies of 82-141 cells fill 22-54% of their bounding boxes (136-330 sites). Each cell does 0.50 GRN ticks, 2.7-2.8 morphogen packets, 0.03-0.12 spikes and 0.17-0.69 spike arrivals per unit time. The shortest inter-spike interval is 0.50, the refractory floor. CPU cost is 0.070-0.119 s per life on the loaded laptop.
findings.evidence: MEASURED: hw_measure.py, giving hw_measure_summary.json and hw_measure_raw.json. Ledger n_end (127, 140.5, 82, 102.5) matches the reconstructed body sizes, and cell-units per life are 55k-122k, consistent with the audit. A dense per-body tensor therefore wastes 2-5x on a bounding box and 8-12x on the full n_max=1024 lattice.

findings.claim: Time-stepping adds a model clock, and that clock changes event order measurably. At dt=1/16, 3.2-4.6% of spikes have a lattice neighbour's spike in the same bin; at dt=1/64 it is 0.7-1.1%; the fraction scales roughly linearly with dt. No cell's own spikes merge for dt <= 0.5. The audit found that the clockless dynamics decorrelate after any change, so a stepped model can only match the reference statistically (F distributions), never life by life.
findings.evidence: MEASURED: nb_samebin_frac in hw_measure_summary.json (speck_s5 0.0457 / 0.0107, speck_s0 0.0321 / 0.0074, v1 L4 s5 0.0424 / 0.0104, speck_s2 0.0362 / 0.0092 at dt 1/16 / 1/64). Decorrelation is from compute_audit.json ('samples' area).

findings.claim: Cloud FPGAs: AWS EC2 F2 (AMD Virtex UltraScale+ HBM VU47P, 16 GB HBM per FPGA) is the main rental option. f2.6xlarge (1 FPGA) costs $1.98/h on demand and $0.659/h spot; f2.48xlarge (8 FPGAs) costs $15.84 and $4.80. The F2 shell clock is fixed at 250 MHz. Supported tools are Vivado 2024.1-2025.2, with both the HDK (RTL, Small Shell, 88% of resources usable) and Vitis (C/C++/HLS and RTL kernels) flows. Azure's FPGA NP-series (Alveo U250) retires on 2027-05-31.

findings.evidence: SOURCED (2026-10-09): neuroAIx (Kauth et al. 2023) used 35 NetFPGA SUME boards at 189 MHz to run a 77,169-neuron, 0.3B-synapse microcircuit at dt 0.1 ms, 20.36x real time, 48 nJ per synaptic event (NEST 1.88x, SpiNNaker 1.0x) https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fncom.2023.1144143/full . findings.claim: Prior work on development and evolvable hardware shows the model's ideas in silicon: genome-carrying cells, self-repair and growth in FPGA tissues. It is small, synchronous, and decades old.
findings.evidence: SOURCED: POEtic (EU IST-2000-28027, 2001-09-01 to 2005-02-15, EUR 1.6M) built a tissue with genotype, configuration and phenotype planes for phylogenesis, ontogenesis and epigenesis https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/IST-2000-28027 . findings.claim: Loihi 2 has the right primitives: microcode-programmable neurons, graded spikes, about 1M neurons per chip and an asynchronous design. Access and tooling are now the problem: Intel archived Lava on 2026-05-13, the next SDK is not public, and access requires joining INRC. Algorithmic time on Loihi advances in global timesteps, which is a model clock, and synapses cannot be created at run time, so growth means pre-allocating every lattice slot.
findings.evidence: SOURCED: 126-128 neuro cores, 6 embedded cores, up to 8,190 neurons per core, graded spikes up to 24-bit, 'an asynchronous, brain-inspired research processor' https://arxiv.org/html/2310.03251 . Hala Point (2024-04-17): 1,152 chips, 1.15B neurons, 2,600 W https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/newsroom/news/intel-builds-worlds-largest-neuromorphic-system.html . Lava archived 2026-05-13 with no maintenance https://github.com/lava-nc/lava . INRC membership is 'free and open to all qualified groups' https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/research/neuromorphic-computing.html . ESTIMATED: 17-204 bodies per chip, assuming 20-60 compartments per site and 256-1,024 sites. I could not verify the timestep rate, so I give no throughput figure.

findings.claim: SpiNNaker2 matches the model's semantics best: programmable ARM cores, local multicast packets, asynchronous execution between cores, and growth done in software. It is not a throughput win for the exact kernel because its cores lack float64.
findings.evidence: SOURCED: 152 Cortex-M4F cores per chip, 128 kB SRAM each, 2 GB DRAM per chip, 6 links to neighbouring chips, 48 chips per board, more than 35k chips built, largest system about 5M PEs; 'encourages autonomous and asynchronous execution between cores'; the Dresden system is 'remotely available to interested researchers' and systems are 'commercially available' https://arxiv.org/html/2401.04491 . SpiNNcloud lists no prices https://spinncloud.com/ . Structural plasticity on SpiNNaker1 rewires synapses at run time within pre-allocated slots https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2018.00434/full . ESTIMATED (core clock not verified): 0.8-4.6 laptop-core equivalents per chip, 36-220 per board.

findings.claim: BrainScaleS-2 is the only platform that has already run in-the-loop evolution of an embodied spiking agent with the environment on chip. It is analog and accelerated, so it is not reproducible bit for bit, and it is small.
findings.evidence: SOURCED: Pehle et al. 2022 describe 512 AdEx neuron circuits and 2^17 synapses per ASIC, 1000x faster than biology, and two plasticity processors (SIMD, 128x8-bit or 64x16-bit vectors) that change weights, topology and parameters during continuous-time operation and simulate environments. Evolving an insect-navigation agent (200 generations x 1,000 individuals) took about 12 h instead of 448 days https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11063 (text saved as bss2.txt). DERIVED: about 4.6 evaluations per second per setup, roughly 0.4 laptop cores at our life cost.

findings.claim: SynSense Speck/Xylo, IBM TrueNorth and IBM NorthPole cannot host this model. All have fixed network topologies, none supports growth or a programmable per-cell GRN, and NorthPole does not spike and runs inference only.
findings.evidence: SOURCED: Speck has 330,000 neurons, under 2 mW, CNNs of up to 9 layers, and an integrated DVS https://www.synsense.ai/products/speck-2/ . Xylo is a microwatt SRNN programmed with Rockpool https://www.synsense.ai/products/xylo/ . NorthPole is 12 nm with 256 cores and 8/4/2-bit precision, 'only for inferencing', and not commercially available https://research.ibm.com/blog/northpole-ibm-ai-chip . TrueNorth has 4,096 cores x 256 neurons and 268M synapses at about 70 mW https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cognitive_computer

findings.claim: GPU simulators only pay off with large networks or very large batches; per-life networks of 100-300 cells are too small on their own. A GPU version of cell-dev would need one persistent kernel with one thread block per life, batching thousands of lives.
findings.evidence: SOURCED: Brian2CUDA is about 1,000x faster than 1-thread C++ for N > 1e5, but is slower for small networks because kernel-launch overhead dominates, and heterogeneous delays cost 1-3 orders of magnitude https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fninf.2022.883700/full . GeNN on a V100 runs the microcircuit at about 0.5x real time https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2018.00941/full . CAX (JAX) is up to 2,000x faster than CellPyLib, but only 1.5x faster than TF for an NCA, on an RTX A6000 https://arxiv.org/html/2410.02651 . EvoJAX finishes in 'minutes on a single accelerator vs hours or days on CPUs' https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.05008 . Runpod rents an RTX 4090 at $0.89/h and an H100 SXM at $3.99/h https://www.runpod.io/pricing

findings.claim: Prototyping an ASIC is now cheap and fast enough for a tile-per-cell experiment.
findings.evidence: SOURCED (2026-10-09): Tiny Tapeout charges EUR 70 per tile and EUR 300 per devkit (EUR 100 subsidy), plus EUR 15 shipping (price constants in https://app.tinytapeout.com/_build/assets/invoice-WoZjomWD.js). A tile is about 1,000 gates (160x110 um on SKY130, 350x160 um on GF180). Open shuttles: TTSKY26d (deadline 2026-11-30) and TTGF26c/d (deadline 2026-12-07), delivery about 2027-06-09 https://tinytapeout.com/chips/ . wafer.space (GF180MCU) sells a 20.12 mm2 slot for $7k early / $8k standard and a 4.9 mm2 slot for $2k/$3k, 1,000 dies each, shipping Q2 2027 https://wafer.space/ . ChipFoundry chipIgnite (SKY130) is $14,950 for 15 mm2 and 100 parts; CI2612 commits 2026-11-04 and delivers 2027-05-25 https://chipfoundry.io/ . findings.claim: For a tile-per-cell chip, storing the genome in each cell takes most of the area, while the cell's computation is tiny. At 1 model unit = 1 ms, a cell needs about 0.38 M MAC/s, which a serial 8-bit MAC at about 1 MHz covers. 875 eight-bit genome parameters (7 kbit) stored in flip-flops take about 0.13-0.18 mm2 in SKY130, so a 15 mm2 chipIgnite die holds roughly 40-75 cells. A Tiny Tapeout tile can hold only a toy cell with a genome of a few dozen bits.
findings.evidence: MEASURED: 0.50 ticks per cell per unit (hw_estimates.json per_cell); spec gives 16x25 + 23x16 = 768 MACs per tick. ESTIMATED/UNVERIFIED: SKY130 DFF area is 18-25 um2 (from memory), and 0.2-0.4 mm2 per cell is assumed. Copying the genome to the daughter over the neighbour link at division keeps storage local; Embryonics cells likewise carried the whole genome (from memory, UNVERIFIED).

findings.claim: Speed does not limit embodiment. One laptop core runs a body of 82-141 cells 8.6-14.7x faster than real time if 1 model unit = 1 ms. A microcontroller or a small FPGA could drive one body in real time.
findings.evidence: MEASURED: 68-116 us of loaded-laptop CPU per model unit (hw_estimates.json per_cell). ASSUMPTION: an MCU is 10-20x slower per core than the laptop on this code.

findings.claim: There are three senses of 'clock' in hardware, and only the second one breaks the model. (1) A clocked discrete-event engine (CPU today, or an FPGA at 250 MHz) that carries event times as data: the clock sets only speed, and behaviour stays clockless and replayable. (2) Lockstep time-stepping (a GPU with dt; Loihi algorithmic timesteps; the usual SpiNNaker 1 ms timers): behaviour depends on dt and on how events within a step are ordered. (3) Physical-time silicon (asynchronous or analog: BrainScaleS-2, DYNAP-SE2, GALS tiles with free-running local oscillators): truly clockless, but not reproducible bit for bit, and evolution may exploit quirks of one chip.
findings.evidence: SOURCED examples: DYNAP-SE2 has 1,024 analog neurons in 180 nm with 'clock-free asynchronous digital hierarchical routing' in native real time https://arxiv.org/html/2310.00564 . Asynchronous processor history (Caltech QDI 1988, AMULET, TrueNorth 2014) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asynchronous_circuit . The open-source ACT asynchronous flow https://avlsi.csl.yale.edu/act/doku.php . MEASURED cost of (2): 0.7-4.6% of spikes have a neighbour's spike in the same bin at dt 1/64 to 1/16. UNVERIFIED: no asynchronous FPGA appears to be on sale today; Achronix moved its async picoPIPE fabric to synchronous parts.

options.option: Status quo: keep the exact event-driven CPU kernel, add the exact 'fast' mode, and rent many-core CPU boxes
options.speedup_or_benefit: 1.24-1.35x from the fast mode (audit). One c8a.48xlarge is about 500 laptop-equivalents (L-eq), so a pilot takes 1-1.5 h instead of about 24 h. $0.0085-0.011 per L-h on spot.
options.semantic_changes: None: exact, clockless, bitwise reproducible. Image pinning and the libm FMA variant need care across machines.
options.effort: Days: add resume, pin the image, build the fast mode (C/Python skills).
options.cost: About $6-16 per pilot; about $22-59 for a 2,200 L-h ablation (audit, 2026-10-09).
options.risks: Bitwise drift across CPUs and glibc versions; serial generation chain limits latency to about 32 threads per run.

options.option: FPGA port of the exact float64 kernel, bitwise equal to glibc libm
options.speedup_or_benefit: Estimated 0.5-3x per dollar at best. Double-precision exp/log/tanh that reproduces glibc's table-plus-polynomial algorithms costs many DSPs, and one life's event loop is serial at 250 MHz against a 4-5 GHz CPU.
options.semantic_changes: None in principle, but the FPGA must reproduce glibc's exact algorithms and FMA variant.
options.effort: 6-12 person-months of expert RTL/HLS (estimate).
options.cost: F2 at $0.66-1.98/h per FPGA plus engineering of about $60k-240k (estimate).
options.risks: Very high: every kernel change must be re-verified bit for bit in hardware. Not recommended.

options.option: FPGA fixed-point, event-driven redesign: time-multiplexed 'life engines' with a 16-lane GRN tick engine and a hardware event queue, carrying timestamps as data
options.speedup_or_benefit: Estimated 350-4,200 L-eq per VU47P FPGA (169-338 engines at 250 MHz, 7-43 ms per life per engine). That is 5-70x cheaper per unit of work than spot CPUs (f2.6xlarge spot $0.659/h), and an f2.48xlarge is about 2,800-33,000 L-eq, 6-67x a c8a box per wall-hour. It saves only about $1.4-2.4 per pilot at today's scale.
options.semantic_changes: A new integer ABI: quantised time (for example 2^-k units), fixed-point state, lookup-table exp/sigmoid, a cheap counter-based RNG. It stays event-driven and clockless; the 250 MHz clock only sets throughput. The C/Python reference must be rewritten to match the FPGA bit for bit, and evolved genomes may behave differently, so it needs a statistical equivalence check.
options.effort: 4-9 person-months (estimate): HLS for the GRN engine, RTL for the event queue, the F2 AFI flow, verification. It must track planned model changes (radius 2, per-channel face weights, gene duplication).
options.cost: $0.66/h spot per FPGA; $40k-180k engineering (estimate, $10-20k per person-month).
options.risks: The model keeps changing while the FPGA design chases it; long Vivado builds; F2 clock fixed at 250 MHz; VU47P resource numbers unverified; host/DMA overhead not modelled.

options.option: GPU time-stepped reformulation: one thread block per life, dense per-body hex tensor of about 256 sites, fine dt, per-cell jittered tick phases, delay ring buffers, masked and compacted GRN ticks, thousands of lives per launch
options.speedup_or_benefit: Estimated 55-2,400 L-eq per RTX 4090 at dt=1/16 (0.5-30x cheaper per unit of work than spot CPUs at $0.89/h), and 14-590 L-eq at dt=1/64 (0.13-7x). One generation of about 1,070 lives fills one GPU in about 1.4 waves.
options.semantic_changes: Introduces a model clock (lockstep dt). 3-5% (dt 1/16) or about 1% (dt 1/64) of spikes coincide in a bin with a neighbour's spike and get ordered by convention (measured). float32 or fixed point. It can only match the exact model statistically. Usable as an approximate screening model, with final selection on the exact CPU kernel.
options.effort: 1.5-3 person-months in CUDA, Triton or JAX (estimate), plus a statistical equivalence study.
options.cost: $0.89-3.99/h per GPU (Runpod); $15k-60k engineering (estimate).
options.risks: Violates the 'no central clock' requirement unless it is treated as an approximation. Divergence and occupancy at about 30-50% fill; small networks pay launch overhead (Brian2CUDA); results differ across GPU models unless reductions are fixed.

options.option: SpiNNaker2 (software cells on ARM M4F cores; local multicast spikes and morphogen messages; growth in software)
options.speedup_or_benefit: No throughput gain: estimated 0.8-4.6 L-eq per chip, 36-220 per 48-chip board. The benefit is semantic. It is the closest existing machine to 'cells as processors exchanging local messages': GALS (globally asynchronous, locally synchronous) design, asynchronous execution between cores, per-core frequency scaling.
options.semantic_changes: No float64 (the M4F has only single-precision floating point), so it needs the fixed-point ABI. It can stay event-driven and clockless if the usual 1 ms timer loop is avoided. Growth needs pre-allocated cell slots and routing entries.
options.effort: 3-6 person-months to write a custom event-driven application (estimate), plus access negotiation.
options.cost: Unknown: SpiNNcloud lists no prices; remote access to the Dresden system is offered to researchers (arXiv 2401.04491).
options.risks: Opaque access and pricing; small user community for non-PyNN applications; core clock and toolchain details unverified.

options.option: Intel Loihi 2 via INRC
options.speedup_or_benefit: Capacity for about 17-204 bodies per chip (estimate). Throughput is unknown because the timestep rate is unverified. Energy efficiency is likely high.
options.semantic_changes: Global algorithmic timesteps form a model clock. Synapses cannot be created at run time, so the whole lattice must be pre-allocated. The GRN has to be written in neuron microcode with graded spikes (up to 24-bit integers) or run on the 6 embedded cores. Integer arithmetic only.
options.effort: 4-8 person-months (estimate).
options.cost: Free INRC membership for qualified groups; hardware cannot be bought.
options.risks: High: Lava was archived on 2026-05-13 and the next SDK is not public; access depends on Intel; vendor lock-in.

options.option: BrainScaleS-2 (EBRAINS): accelerated analog in-the-loop evolution of small bodies, with the plasticity processors handling growth, the GRN and the world
options.speedup_or_benefit: 1000x faster than biological time, with a demonstrated embodied-evolution workflow (200 x 1,000 evaluations in about 12 h, about 4.6 per second per setup). About 0.4 L-eq at our life cost, so the benefit is physical-time, clockless dynamics, not throughput.
options.semantic_changes: Analog AdEx neurons in physical time: no model clock, but not reproducible bit for bit, and chips differ by mismatch. At most 512 neurons per chip, so bodies are capped well below n_max. The GRN on the PPU may limit the time-unit mapping.
options.effort: 2-4 person-months (estimate), plus calibration.
options.cost: Research access via EBRAINS (current terms unverified).
options.risks: Evolution may fit one chip's quirks (Thompson 1996); small capacity; access queues.

options.option: SynSense Speck/Xylo, IBM TrueNorth, IBM NorthPole
options.speedup_or_benefit: None for this model. Speck could at most serve as a DVS sensor front end for a future robot body.
options.semantic_changes: Fixed CNN/SRNN topologies, no growth, no per-cell GRN. NorthPole does not spike.
options.effort: Not applicable
options.cost: Dev kit prices not public (unverified); TrueNorth and NorthPole not for sale.
options.risks: Not suitable.

options.option: Tile-per-cell ASIC (silicon-retina style): GALS tiles with free-running local oscillators (the jittered tick), or QDI asynchronous logic; genome copied to the daughter over the neighbour link at division
options.speedup_or_benefit: Real time at microwatts; truly local and clockless in the physical sense. About 0.38 M MAC/s per cell at 1 unit = 1 ms, so a serial MAC at about 1 MHz suffices. About 40-75 full-genome cells on a 15 mm2 SKY130 die (estimate).
options.semantic_changes: Fixed-point and physical time, not reproducible bit for bit. Tiles are fixed, so growth means waking dormant tiles. The neighbour wiring sets the radius (a radius-2 gene needs extra links).
options.effort: A Tiny Tapeout toy cell takes 1-2 person-months; a small array (wafer.space or chipIgnite) about 6-12 person-months (estimate). Asynchronous design needs the ACT flow and expertise.
options.cost: Tiny Tapeout EUR 70 per tile plus EUR 300 devkit; wafer.space $2k-8k for 1,000 dies (GF180); chipIgnite $14,950 for 15 mm2 and 100 parts; Europractice IHP 130 nm 7,300 EUR/mm2. Turnaround 6-12 months.
options.risks: Long turnaround; the genome-storage area dominates; analog and timing variability; designing before the model stabilises.

options.option: Real-time embodiment on a microcontroller or a small FPGA board (one body, one life, driving a real or simulated body)
options.speedup_or_benefit: A laptop core already runs about 100-cell bodies 9-15x faster than real time at 1 unit = 1 ms (measured), so one MCU or a small FPGA can run a body in real time.
options.semantic_changes: None if the CPU kernel is reused (float64 on an MCU with a double FPU); otherwise the fixed-point ABI.
options.effort: Weeks (estimate).
options.cost: Tens to hundreds of dollars of hardware (unverified).
options.risks: Low; but it tests embodiment, not throughput.

recommendations: Do not build accelerator hardware to speed up evolution now. Rent CPUs: a pilot costs $6-16, and even an optimistic FPGA saves about $2 per pilot. Revisit when planned studies exceed about $5-10k of compute, for example if ranking near-neutral mutants needs 70-200 lives per genome (audit).

The first hardware step is in software: define an integer 'hardware ABI' variant of the kernel (integer time in 2^-k units, fixed-point state, lookup-table exp/sigmoid, a cheap counter-based RNG), keep it event-driven, and test on CPUs whether evolved mechanisms survive (paired F distributions). Every FPGA, ASIC or neuromorphic path depends on this, and it also removes the libm/FMA cross-machine risk.

Write down a 'cell budget' per cell: bits of state, MACs per tick, messages per unit, neighbour slots. Treat it as a design constraint. The planned radius-2 gene, per-channel face weights and gene duplication raise wiring and storage per tile, so check each against this budget.

State the clock policy explicitly in docs/LIFE_ABI.md. A hardware clock is allowed when event times are data and results do not depend on processing order (as on the CPU today, or a 250 MHz FPGA engine). Lockstep dt is an approximation, measured here to reorder 0.7-4.6% of neighbour spike pairs at dt 1/64 to 1/16. Physical-time silicon is the eventual clockless target and gives up bitwise replay.

If a hardware prototype is wanted, start with an FPGA cell or life engine (AWS F2 spot at $0.66/h, or a dev board), using HLS for the GRN tick and RTL for the event queue. Validate it bit for bit against the integer ABI reference. Copy Wang et al. 2018's time multiplexing for scale.

For the long-term 'cells as circuits' goal, plan a staged silicon path: (1) one reduced cell on Tiny Tapeout (EUR 70 per tile; the next deadlines are 2026-11-30 and 2026-12-07) to learn the flow; (2) a GALS array of 30-75 full cells on wafer.space ($2-8k) or chipIgnite ($14,950); (3) look at asynchronous (QDI, ACT flow) tiles only after that. Keep the genome local by copying it to the daughter at division, as Embryonics did.

Among neuromorphic platforms, ask SpiNNcloud and TU Dresden about remote SpiNNaker2 access (best semantic fit) and look at BrainScaleS-2 via EBRAINS for physical-time in-the-loop evolution of small bodies. Do not invest in Loihi 2 until Intel publishes the successor to Lava, and skip SynSense, TrueNorth and NorthPole.

Build a GPU time-stepped version only as a declared approximate screening model, with final selection and validation on the exact kernel. Its estimated gain (about 0.5-30x per dollar at dt 1/16) does not justify breaking the no-central-clock rule for the main pipeline.

Verify before budgeting: VU47P resources, Alveo card prices, the Europractice per-mm2 figures (checked only against a fetched summary), Loihi 2 timestep rates, the SpiNNaker2 core clock and access terms, and any NCA-on-FPGA work. The WebSearch budget ran out in this session, so these could not be checked.

verdict.title: Skeptic re-check of the platform survey: the cost verdict holds, but a model clock is not required and two figures are off by about 2x

checks.claim: Hardware acceleration does not pay off for evolution throughput. A pilot is about 217 L-h, $2-16 of CPU, and an FPGA saves only about $1.4-2.4 per pilot.
checks.recheck: Redid the arithmetic in verify/recompute.py. Reread the audit's scale-out area (results/catch_pilot/compute_audit.json). Rebuilt the FPGA saving from my own FPGA estimate (check 4).
checks.result: At fully used spot prices, 217 L-h x $0.0085-0.0111 = $1.84-2.41 (measured inputs). The $6-16 figure is what one c8a box costs for the pilot, including idle tail time (audit: $8 spot, $16 on-demand; Modal about $6). With my lower FPGA throughput the saving is $0.9-2.4 per pilot (estimate). A 100x study costs $184-241 on spot CPUs. Engineering at $40k-180k is the study's assumption, but any plausible cost leaves break-even at thousands of pilots.

checks.claim: Every faster platform needs a new integer/fixed-point ABI or a time-stepped approximation, and the GPU route brings a model clock (summary; findings 2 and 4; the GPU option).
checks.recheck: Read LIFE_ABI.md sections 11.1-11.2, 13 and 15.42, and the window scheduler in kernel.c (run_window, line 1900). Ran 4 evolved pilot bests x 6 lives (T=1024, seeds fresh_seeds(6, seed0=37,600,000)) under the heap scheduler and under the window scheduler at h=0.5 and h=0.25, with order seeds 1 and 7 (verify/check_bins.py, check_bins.json).
checks.result: MEASURED: ledger and hashes are bitwise identical in 96 of 96 comparisons (4 bodies x 6 lives x 2 h x 2 order seeds). The repo already has an exact parallel schedule: time windows of h <= d_min = 0.5. Within one window every site processes its own events in any order (the contract says the result is identical 'for any tie seed, order seed'), and messages land only in later windows. That is conservative parallel simulation with lookahead d_min. Parallel hardware (GPU blocks, FPGA engines, one tile per cell) can therefore stay event-driven, without a model clock, and bitwise reproducible. The window barrier, or a purely local neighbour-to-neighbour sync with lookahead d_min, is only an implementation clock. MEASURED: 40-100 heap events per window per life is the parallelism available inside one life. Separately, the integer ABI the study proposes is already reserved as the 'integer twin' in LIFE_ABI.md section 13 (int64 time in 2^-20 units, Q24 g and m, lookup-table exp and ln). Only the float64/glibc dependence forces a new ABI. Time stepping is never forced.

checks.claim: Time-stepping reorders events measurably: at dt=1/16, 3.2-4.6% of spikes have a lattice neighbour's spike in the same bin; at dt=1/64, 0.7-1.1%.
checks.recheck: Recomputed on fresh seeds (37,600,000+). I also computed (a) the two-sided fraction of spikes with at least one same-bin neighbour spike, and (b) the fraction of spike arrivals at a cell that share a bin with an arrival from another source or with the cell's own spike. (b) is what a lockstep step actually merges. Delays were drawn like LIFE_ABI 7.3, with the delta knob ignored.
checks.result: MEASURED: the study's own metric reproduces (3.2-5.1% at 1/16, 0.7-1.3% at 1/64). But it counts each neighbour pair from one side only, so it understates by about 2x. Two-sided: 6.1-9.3% of spikes at 1/16, 1.4-2.5% at 1/64. Arrivals that share a bin with another input or with the target's spike: 6.2-9.9% at 1/16, 1.6-2.7% at 1/64. Both scale roughly linearly with dt. The study's claim that a cell's own spikes never merge for dt <= 0.5 holds (minimum ISI 0.50000038).
