verdict.corrected_summary:
The study's headline answer holds: custom hardware could run cell-dev lives faster, but for evolution throughput today it does not pay. A pilot is 217 L-h, which is $1.84-2.41 at fully used spot CPU prices and $6-16 as actually rented on one box. My re-estimate of a fixed-point event-driven FPGA engine on an AWS F2 VU47P is 160-2,700 laptop-core equivalents (the study said 350-4,200). That is 2-45x cheaper per unit of work and saves $0.9-2.4 per pilot, against months of engineering. The study's figure was inflated by mismatched min/mean pairing, by ignoring on-chip memory (only about 90-380 lives can be resident), and by assuming 2-8 cycles per event inside one serial life.

A time-stepped GPU version is weaker than claimed. My estimate is 21-1,350 L-eq at dt=1/16 and 5-340 at dt=1/64 (the study said 55-2,400 and 14-590): its op counts were set against an FMA-doubled FLOPS peak, and its 256-site tensor is smaller than the measured 330-site bounding box. Its semantic cost is also about 2x larger than reported. Measured: 6-10% of spike arrivals at a cell share a dt=1/16 bin with another input or with the cell's own spike, and 1.6-2.7% at dt=1/64. The study reported 3-5% and about 1%.

The main correction concerns clocks and exactness. Time stepping is never required. The repo's window scheduler (LIFE_ABI 11.2) processes all sites in windows of h <= d_min = 0.5 in any order, and I measured it bitwise identical to the heap scheduler on 96 of 96 evolved-body comparisons. So parallel hardware (a GPU block per life, multi-engine FPGAs, or tile-per-cell chips with only neighbour-to-neighbour sync using lookahead d_min) can be event-driven, free of any model clock, local and bitwise reproducible. The only change it needs is to drop float64/glibc for the integer twin already reserved in LIFE_ABI section 13 (int64 time in 2^-20 units, Q24 state, lookup-table exp and ln). This gives a fourth sense of 'clock' beyond the study's three: a hardware clock or barrier that sets only speed, even in a parallel or tile design. Physical-time analog or asynchronous silicon is a separate choice that gives up replay; it is not the only clockless route.

Revised recommendations:
1. Keep renting CPUs.
2. Build the integer twin plus a window-scheduled reference first, and test on CPUs whether evolved mechanisms survive.
3. If you want hardware, prototype a window-synchronous engine on GPU or FPGA, validated bit for bit against the twin. Use the time-stepped GPU only as a declared approximation, if at all.
4. For silicon, note that the genome's area cost depends on design. A per-cell copy uses 0.19-0.26 mm2 in SKY130, but one shared streamed copy is possible. A full cell fits in one Tiny Tapeout 8x2 or 8x4 slot (EUR 1,120-2,240), not just a toy.

Confirmed as stated: F2 prices ($1.98 on-demand / $0.659 spot; $15.84 / $4.799), the 250 MHz shell clock (but design logic may use other clocks), chipIgnite ($14,950, 15 mm2), Lava archived on 2026-05-13, the BrainScaleS-2 figures, and real-time embodiment margin (8.6-14.7x).

Unverified: VU47P resource counts, RTX 4090 specs, SKY130 DFF area, and every engineering-effort figure. WebSearch was exhausted; external facts were checked with WebFetch on 2026-10-09.
verdict.missed:
1. The study missed the existing window scheduler (LIFE_ABI 11.2, kernel.c run_window). It gives exact parallelism with lookahead d_min and an order-independence guarantee. This is the central fact for 'local cell logic on hardware'. Each site needs only its own state plus neighbour messages older than d_min, so tiles can use local conservative sync with no global clock and still replay bit for bit. Only the global accountant (world physics) needs a wider sync.
2. The integer ABI the study proposes is already specified in LIFE_ABI section 13 as the 'integer twin'. The recommendation should build on it, not reinvent it.
3. In any parallel design, the per-life accountant (canonical record sort, dot physics, hash folds) is a serial step that limits speedup (Amdahl). Fixed-point sums are associative, which allows parallel reduction; float64 sums are not. Hash folds serve verification only (audit: 9.3% of CPU).
4. CPU-side gains were underused. Receptor candidates are about 25% of CPU and 95% are rejected in SPECK (audit), so a tighter thinning bound in the next ABI is cheap. An integer twin on CPU is probably faster than float64 too, which shrinks the FPGA's relative lead.
5. A fixed GPU tensor or FPGA provisioning caps body size. Bodies at T=1536 reach 290 cells, and founder lives hit the n_max=1024 guard, so overflow handling must not silently add a new growth rule.
6. On a GALS tile chip, a shared streamed read-only genome is possible. A correctly rounded libm such as CORE-MATH could be an alternative path to cross-platform float64 exactness (from memory, not verified).
7. Tiny Tapeout multi-tile slots of up to 8x4 can hold a full cell.
8. f2.48xlarge carries 192 host vCPUs that could run lives too.
9. The serial generation chain means latency per generation, not just throughput, sets wall time. Window-parallel designs help latency because they parallelise inside one life.
Files are in /tmp/claude-1000/-home-jgon-project-ml-cell-dev/aefb0c66-3af5-49c4-936c-154d6434706c/scratchpad/hw/platforms/verify/: check_bins.py and check_bins.json (time bins and the window-vs-heap bitwise check), recompute.py and recompute.json (cost, FPGA, GPU and ASIC estimates).

report.title: Would custom hardware make cell-dev evolution faster? A throughput and cost model for CPU, integer CPU, time-stepped GPU, FPGA and neuromorphic chips (pilot-120 workload, 2026-10-09)
report.summary: Yes, some hardware could run the task faster, but at today's scale none of it pays for its engineering. The model uses a "pilot-120" workload: 29 runs x 500 generations x 1,070 lives of 120-cell bodies at T=1100, about 768 laptop-CPU-hours. One rented 192-core AWS c7a box runs that in about 2.1 h for about $7 at spot price ($21 on-demand). A time-stepped GPU rewrite might be 4-14x faster per GPU than that box and 5-17x cheaper per dollar (estimated). The price is the clockless design: all cells would update in lockstep at a step size dt, and behaviour would then depend on dt. An FPGA built from "life engines" (one small processor per life, with its cells' state in on-chip memory) would give about 1,000 lives/s per chip. That is about half a CPU box per FPGA and up to about 2.5x cheaper per life on spot. An array with one processor per lattice site, the literal "cells as circuits", runs one body very quickly but gives only about 260 lives/s per FPGA, because most sites are empty and most processors sit idle. SpiNNaker2 (about 110 lives/s per chip) and Loihi 2 cannot be rented by the hour and would not speed up evolution. A pilot costs $7-21 in CPU rental, so even the cheapest change, the existing exact fast mode, needs about 1,400 pilots to pay back its person-week. The GPU and integer-kernel routes need about 4,000-5,000 pilots, and FPGA engines about 18,000. The one step that helps both throughput and the long-term hardware goal is an integer/fixed-point version of the model's contract, a new ABI 4: integer time, fixed-point state, lookup tables instead of libm, and order-free integer sums. On CPUs it should give about 1.6-2.6x (estimated from microbenchmarks). It also makes results bitwise identical across machines, and gives any later FPGA, GPU or ASIC build an exact CPU reference to check against. A hardware clock is fine as an implementation detail: integer timestamps and barriers every d_min = 0.5 keep the model exact and clockless. Only lockstep dt-stepping (time-stepped GPU, Loihi 2) puts the clock into the model.

findings.claim: Baseline: pilot-120 costs about 768 loaded-laptop CPU-hours. On one AWS c7a.48xlarge (192 Zen 4 cores) the current kernel runs about 2,030 lives/s (1,790-2,290), so a pilot takes 2.1 h (1.9-2.4) and costs $7.2 at spot or $20.9 on-demand. On a c8a.48xlarge it takes 1.6 h and costs $9.1 spot or $16.9 on-demand.
findings.evidence: Measured (audit): 1.2-1.5 us per cell-unit on a loaded laptop E-core. Workload: 15,515,000 lives x 132,000 cell-units, giving 683-853 laptop-CPU-h (the task's 29 x 24 = 696 is inside that range). Estimated (audit): a rented core is 2.0x (1.6-2.4) the loaded laptop core on c7a and 2.6x on c8a; box efficiency 0.90-0.98. Sourced: c7a.48xlarge $9.853/h on-demand, $3.398/h spot; c8a.48xlarge $10.346 / $5.549 (instances.vantage.sh, fetched 2026-10-09). Monte Carlo p10-p90 in raw/model_output.json. Dominant uncertainty: the rented core's speed (1.5x swing). It can be measured in 10 minutes on the box.

findings.claim: Measured today on a lightly loaded laptop, the exact kernel is 1.5-2.9x faster than the audit's loaded baseline. That fits the audit's 2.0x factor for a server core.
findings.evidence: Measured (pin_bench.py, raw/pin_bench.jsonl; speck s5 best genome, T=1100, 8 fresh lives, seeds from 37,100,000; load 2.4): P-core cpu0 at 4.99 GHz: 0.069 s per life, 0.516 us/cell-unit. E-cores cpu6/cpu9 at 4.0-4.1 GHz: 0.107 s, 0.80 us/cell-unit. Unpinned over 5 bodies: 0.49-0.59 us/cell-unit (raw/body_stats.json). Seed base: the task template printed '[object Object]1'; I used 37,000,000 + 100,000 x 1.

findings.claim: The workload is sparse events plus messaging, not arithmetic. Per cell-time unit there are 0.50 GRN ticks, 2.6-2.95 morphogen packets, 1.3-2.7 scheduler events, 0.017-0.12 spikes and 0.84-1.18 receptor candidates, of which only 3.5-4.9% are accepted in SPECK. All GRN arithmetic in one life is about 0.1 GFLOP, so FLOPs never limit any platform.
findings.evidence: Measured (body_stats.py, raw/body_stats.json): 5 evolved bodies (SPECK s0/s4/s5/s6, v1 s5), 8 lives each at T=1100. Example, speck s5: 133,823 cell-units, 67,014 ticks, 372,784 packets, 6,034 spikes, 34,338 arrivals, 127,135 receptor candidates, 5,443 accepted. Every pilot genome has 8 active genes (lam != 0), and all lam values are powers of two. Bodies span hex radius 4-7 and use planes 0-3. Estimated arithmetic: 66k ticks x 2 x (16x25 + 23x16) = 0.10 GFLOP per life, which is about 1.5 us on an H100 at 67 TFLOPS.

findings.claim: Lockstep time-stepping is not faster on a CPU. A lean float32 time-stepped prototype costs about the same as the exact event-driven kernel on the same core, because the event kernel does about 1.7 queue events per cell-unit while stepping touches every cell 4-20 times per unit. Any GPU gain must therefore come from the GPU's parallel width, not from a cheaper formulation.
findings.evidence: Measured (ts_proto.c, raw/ts_proto.jsonl; 119-cell final layout of SPECK s5; P-core; FTZ on): per cell-step without GRN ticks 37-39 ns (about 190 cycles; E-core 42-45 ns). One float32 tick (GRN, readout, decode, derive, 8 packets) about 0.44-0.55 us. Per life at T=1100: 0.126 s at dt=0.05, 0.083 s at dt=0.1, 0.059 s at dt=0.25, against 0.069 s for the exact kernel on the same core. Without flush-to-zero, decaying traces hit denormals and the cost rose about 30%.

findings.claim: Fixed-point arithmetic speeds up the model arithmetic 2-4x, but libm is only 10-21% of the tick arithmetic. A full integer kernel is therefore estimated at 1.6-2.6x (mid 2.0x) including fast mode, not more.
findings.evidence: Measured (bench_ops.c, raw/bench_ops_summary.txt; medians of 5-7 interleaved repetitions at load about 11, so ±20% noise). One tick's arithmetic: float64 516 ns vs fixed-point 273 ns on the P-core (536 vs 225 with -march=x86-64-v3); on the E-core 648 vs 304 ns. Replacing exp/log/tanh with cheap stand-ins cuts the float64 tick only 10% (P) to 21% (E). Membrane step: float64 30 ns vs fixed 7.9 ns (P), 39 vs 11.5 (E). Binary heap pop+push at 300 entries: 62-70 ns. Splitmix draw (5 rounds): 4.6 ns (P), 7.3 ns (E). An across-row, vectorisable float64 tick is bitwise identical (0 mismatches in 256,000 ticks) but no faster. Estimated whole-kernel effect, by Amdahl on the audit profile (model arithmetic about 50% of CPU, fast mode removes about 21-26%, integer-key queue about 7%): 1.6-2.6x.

findings.claim: A time-stepped GPU version, with compacted cell lists, state in shared memory and ticks queued for cooperative processing, is estimated at about 15,600 lives/s per H100 at dt=0.1 (9,500-22,800). That is 8,700 at dt=0.05 and 28,600 at dt=0.25. An L4 gives 3,500-11,200. One pilot would cost $0.3-3.4 and take 0.1-1.2 h per GPU. Padding the computation to a dense fixed lattice region cuts throughput about 3x.
findings.evidence: Estimated (throughput_model.py). Lane-slots per life = cell-steps x (170 instructions / 0.75 SIMT efficiency + 20 for queueing) + ticks x 2,200 + per-step overhead: 0.57e9 at dt=0.1. H100 issue peak 33.5e12 lane-instructions/s, i.e. 67 TFLOPS FP32 / 2 (sourced, nvidia.com H100 page, 2026-10-09). Achieved fraction 0.08-0.5. A latency bound (2-8 lives per SM, 1-3 us per step) is also applied. 228 KB shared memory per SM (Hopper tuning guide, 2026-10-09). Sourced prices: H100 $2.89/h (RunPod PCIe), $3.99 (Lambda/RunPod SXM), $6.88 per GPU (AWS p5.48xlarge $55.04/8); L4 $0.59 (RunPod; AWS g6.xlarge spot $0.590) and $0.805 (g6.xlarge on-demand); all fetched 2026-10-09. The cheap H100 price is a PCIe part, about 10-25% slower than SXM. Dominant uncertainty: achieved fraction of peak (6.25x swing), then instructions per cell-step (1.5x). Keeping state in global memory would hit a bandwidth bound of about 12,700 lives/s (264 MB per life at dt=0.1, 3.35 TB/s). Lives growing toward n_max 1024 do not fit in shared memory and need a fallback path or a lower guard.

findings.claim: FPGA (AWS F2, AMD VU47P): life engines are estimated at about 1,000 lives/s per FPGA (735-1,380), i.e. 0.36-0.68 of a c7a box. That is 2.5x the CPU's lives per dollar at F2 spot ($0.659/h) and 0.84x on-demand ($1.98/h). A one-processor-per-site spatial array runs one life in about 3 ms but fits only about 0.8 of a 508-site body region per chip, giving about 260 lives/s per FPGA, 0.13 of a box.
findings.evidence: Estimated (throughput_model.py). Engines: 6-16k LUT, 2-4 DSP and 4-10 URAM each, so 50-200 engines per chip (about 76 at mid). Per life about 17.9M cycles: 66k ticks x (384 MACs / DSPs + 80) + about 225k events x 8 + 368k packets x 1.5, about 77 ms at 250 MHz. Spatial: 1-3k LUT and 1-3 DSP per processor (the task's estimate) gives about 400 processors; each 0.5-unit window costs the slowest processor's tick, about 300 cycles. Sourced: f2.6xlarge $1.98 on-demand, $0.659 spot; f2.48xlarge (8 FPGAs) $15.84 / $4.799 (instances.vantage.sh, 2026-10-09). VU47P FPGAs with 16 GiB HBM (aws.amazon.com/ec2/instance-types/f2, 2026-10-09). 250 MHz shell clock (AWS F2 HDK docs, 2026-10-09). NOT verified: VU47P resources of about 1,304K LUT, 9,024 DSP and 960 URAM are recalled from AMD datasheets, whose pages did not load. Dominant uncertainty: LUTs per engine (2.6x swing) or per processor (3x).

findings.claim: Neuromorphic chips would not speed up evolution, and neither can be rented by the hour. SpiNNaker2 is estimated at about 110 lives/s per chip (75-157), about 0.05 of a CPU box. Loihi 2 throughput cannot be estimated to within about two orders of magnitude without a port. It runs barrier-synchronised time steps (lockstep), its network topology is fixed at compile time (so division would need every site pre-allocated), and the world loop would run on the host or the embedded x86 cores.
findings.evidence: Sourced: SpiNNaker2 has 152 Arm Cortex-M4F cores per chip, 128 kB SRAM per core, 2 GB DRAM per node, exp/log/RNG and 8/16-bit integer MAC accelerators, remote access via SpiNNcloud (arxiv.org/html/2401.04491, fetched 2026-10-09; clock not verified). Loihi 2 has 128 neuron cores, up to 8,192 neurons and 128 KB synaptic memory per core, 6 embedded microprocessors, microcode limited to ADD, MUL_SHR, compare and branch (fixed precision, no sigmoid), 32-bit graded spikes and chip-wide time steps under 200 ns; access only through the free Intel NRC (Intel Loihi 2 brief, download.intel.com/newsroom/2021/new-technologies/neuromorphic-computing-loihi-2-brief.pdf, fetched 2026-10-09). Estimated: one M4F core at 1/15-1/50 of a Zen 4 core on this branchy code, 80% of cores used, integer model assumed.

findings.claim: Break-even against renting CPUs: at $7-21 per pilot-120, the exact fast mode pays back after about 1,400 pilots (600-3,000), the integer ABI after about 4,900 (2,200-13,500), the time-stepped GPU after about 4,700 (1,900-12,000) and FPGA engines after about 18,000 (7,300-46,000). In cumulative rented compute that is roughly $10k, $35k, $34k and $130k of CPU spending. Nothing pays back in dollars at the current scale. The cases for building anything are wall time, much larger future experiments, or the hardware goal itself.
findings.evidence: Estimated. Person-weeks to a first result: fast mode 0.5-1, integer ABI 4-10, GPU time-stepped 6-14, GPU exact-window 12-26, FPGA engines 16-40 (after the integer ABI), FPGA spatial 12-30, SpiNNaker2 8-20, Loihi 2 10-24. Valued at $2,000-5,000 per person-week (an assumption; mid $3,000). Savings are p50 dollars per pilot against the current kernel on c7a spot. Wall time: a CPU box already does a pilot-120 in about 2 h, and 5 boxes cut that to about 0.4 h for the same dollars.

findings.claim: The clock question: the model forbids a global update rule, not a clock inside the machine. Integer-timestamped events, and conservative windows of width d_min = 0.5 with a barrier at each window's end, keep the model exact and clockless. Lockstep dt-stepping (time-stepped GPU, Loihi 2, SpiNNaker's usual 1 ms tick) puts the clock into the model. A free-running physical tissue loses bitwise reproducibility but adds only noise the model already contains.
findings.evidence: From LIFE_ABI.md 6.3 and 11: every message delay is at least d_min, so a site's batch at t depends only on events created before t - d_min, and any causally valid order gives the same history. The window scheduler (h = 2^-k <= d_min) is already tested to be bitwise equal to the heap scheduler. Times are already resolved to 2^-21, so integer time costs nothing semantically. Under dt-stepping, all events within a step become simultaneous and delays, jitter (±0.1), refractory times and receptor timing are rounded to dt. The evolved mechanisms (coincidence windows of about 0.4-1.0 units, one-hop latency about d0) are exactly the dt-sensitive part, so dt would have to be validated as a model parameter. Physical asynchrony maps onto the model's existing noise terms: jit 0.1, delay_sd 0.1, tau_mis 0.05, clock_sd 0.05.

findings.claim: The planned model changes move the hardware costs. A communication radius of 2 multiplies packets and arrivals about 2.5-3x and makes spatial FPGA wiring 2.5-3x bigger. Gene duplication up to 16 active genes doubles the MACs per tick, and ticks are about half of the FPGA and GPU work. Faster conduction (d0 0.5) roughly halves the usable time-stepped dt, and with it GPU throughput.
findings.evidence: Estimated. Hex in-plane neighbours go from 6 to 18 at radius 2. Packets are 5.6 per tick today, about 2.8 per cell-unit. Today's GRN uses 8 of 16 genes (8x25 + 23x8 = 384 MACs); with 16 genes it is 768. GPU cost at small dt scales about 1/dt (model rows dt=0.05 vs 0.1: 8,746 vs 15,578 lives/s).

options.option: (a) Current exact CPU kernel on a rented 192-core box (AWS c7a.48xlarge or c8a.48xlarge)
options.speedup_or_benefit: Baseline. c7a: about 2,030 lives/s per box, 2.1 h and $7.2 spot / $20.9 on-demand per pilot-120. c8a: 1.3x per box in wall time, 1.6 h, $9.1 spot / $16.9 on-demand (0.8x per dollar at spot, 1.24x on-demand). Five boxes cut wall time about 5x for the same dollars.
options.semantic_changes: None. The model stays exact and bitwise identical, provided the same glibc/FMA libm path and torch kernels are used.
options.effort: 0.5-1.5 person-weeks: resume and checkpointing in src/run.py, a pinned image (Ubuntu 24.04, glibc 2.39, ATEN_CPU_CAPABILITY=avx2), and a cross-machine replay check.
options.cost: $3.40-10.35 per box-hour (sourced, 2026-10-09). About $7-21 per pilot-120.
options.risks: The rented core's speed is estimated, not measured (±25%). Spot interruptions lose whole runs until resume exists. Bitwise portability depends on the libm path.

options.option: (b1) Exact fast mode on the same CPU box (no hash folds or per-packet records; sparse readout; x86-64-v3)
options.speedup_or_benefit: 1.24-1.35x (measured by the audit) per box and per dollar: about 2,640 lives/s, 1.6 h and $5.6 spot per pilot-120.
options.semantic_changes: None: the ledger is bitwise identical. Hashes stay at their initial values, so the gates and golden tests must keep using the full build.
options.effort: 0.5-1 person-week. The prototype exists (the audit's opt_patch.py).
options.cost: Same as (a). Engineering about $1.5-5k. Break-even about 1,400 pilots (600-3,000), or about $10k of cumulative CPU spend.
options.risks: Two builds to keep consistent. Hash-based regression checks are lost in production runs.

options.option: (b2/b3) Integer/fixed-point ABI 4 CPU kernel: integer time, Q-format state, lookup tables in place of exp/log/tanh, order-free integer accounting, a hash cheap in hardware; optionally a redesigned receptor candidate stream
options.speedup_or_benefit: Estimated 1.6-2.6x (mid 2.05x) including fast mode, about 4,170 lives/s per box, 1.0 h and $3.5 spot per pilot-120. With the receptor-stream redesign about 2.4x. It also makes results bitwise identical across CPUs and libm builds, and gives any FPGA, GPU or ASIC version an exact reference.
options.semantic_changes: A new ABI: every hash and life changes, so evolution baselines must be re-established. Dynamics stay event-driven and clockless. Tables for sigmoid, exp and log replace libm (bounded error of about 1e-3-1e-4 relative to float64). The receptor redesign keeps the same Poisson law but changes the random streams.
options.effort: 4-10 person-weeks: spec, C kernel, Python reference, tests, re-validating the gates and hand-built bodies, plus a gate that evolved pilot bodies keep F within noise.
options.cost: No new hardware. Engineering about $12-50k. Break-even against CPU dollars about 4,900 pilots (2,200-13,500), or about $35k of spending. The justification is portability and readiness for hardware.
options.risks: The speedup is extrapolated from microbenchmarks (dominant uncertainty, 1.6x swing). Fixed-point ranges must cover evolved weights (|W| up to about 20 in the pilot genomes). Re-baselining costs a pilot.

options.option: (c) Time-stepped GPU version (lockstep dt; one thread per live cell, compacted; state in shared memory; ticks queued and processed cooperatively), H100 or L4
options.speedup_or_benefit: Estimated per GPU against one c7a box: H100 4.3x at dt=0.05, 7.7x at dt=0.1, 14x at dt=0.25 in wall time; 5x, 9x and 17x per dollar at $2.89/h. L4: 1.7-5.5x in wall time, 10-32x per dollar at $0.59/h. About $0.3-3.4 per pilot-120. A dense lattice region instead of a compacted cell list costs about 3x.
options.semantic_changes: Large. The model becomes lockstep at dt: events within a step are simultaneous; delays, ±10% jitter, refractory periods and receptor times are rounded to dt; behaviour depends on dt; float32 arithmetic. This breaks the no-lockstep requirement unless dt is treated as a model parameter with convergence tests (F at dt and dt/2 equal within noise) and transfer tests back to the exact model. Growth beyond the shared-memory budget (about 300-1,000 cells) needs a fallback or a lower n_max guard. All 29 runs must be batched into common generations to fill the GPU.
options.effort: 6-14 person-weeks: a time-stepped spec and a CPU reference, a CUDA kernel with division, death and the dot world, batching across runs, statistical validation. An exact d_min-window GPU kernel (keeps the semantics, needs b2) would take 12-26 person-weeks for an unknown gain.
options.cost: H100 $2.89-6.88 per GPU-hour, L4 $0.59-0.805 (sourced, 2026-10-09). Break-even about 4,700 pilots (1,900-12,000), or about $34k of CPU spend.
options.risks: Dominant uncertainty: the achieved fraction of GPU peak (0.08-0.5, a 6x swing). A 1-2 week CUDA prototype on a rented L4 can measure it. Evolved mechanisms depend on sub-unit timing (coincidence windows of 0.4-1.0, one-hop latency about d0), so dt=0.1-0.25 may change what evolves. Planned faster conduction (d0 0.5) halves the usable dt.

options.option: (d1) FPGA life engines on AWS F2 (VU47P): one small event-driven processor per life, cells of many lives held in on-chip memory, implementing the integer ABI exactly
options.speedup_or_benefit: Estimated about 1,000 lives/s per FPGA (735-1,380): 0.5x of a c7a box per FPGA, about 3.9x per f2.48xlarge (8 FPGAs). Per dollar 2.5x the CPU at F2 spot, 0.84x on-demand. $2.9-8.6 per pilot-120.
options.semantic_changes: None beyond (b2) if the engines implement ABI 4 bitwise. The 250 MHz hardware clock only sequences the work, and the model stays event-driven and clockless.
options.effort: 16-40 person-weeks after (b2): RTL/HLS for the queue, hash, membrane and lookup units, GRN multiply-accumulate sequencer and accountant; the AWS F2 build flow; bitwise co-simulation against the CPU kernel; host integration. Needs FPGA experience.
options.cost: f2.6xlarge $1.98/h on-demand, $0.659 spot; f2.48xlarge $15.84 / $4.80 (sourced, 2026-10-09). Engineering about $50-200k. Break-even about 18,000 pilots, or about $130k of CPU spend.
options.risks: Dominant uncertainty: LUTs per engine (6-16k, a 2.6x swing). VU47P resources not verified. Timing closure at 250 MHz. Long build cycles. AWS tool licensing and shell overhead not checked.

options.option: (d2) FPGA spatial array, one processor per lattice site (cells as circuits, neighbour wires, synchronised every d_min window)
options.speedup_or_benefit: One life in about 3 ms (fast per body), but only about 0.8 of a 508-site body region fits per VU47P with 2k-LUT processors, so about 260 lives/s per FPGA (180-380): 0.13x a CPU box, 0.65x per dollar at spot. Its value is as a demonstrator of the long-term goal, not for evolution: about 24% of sites are occupied and an occupied processor is busy about 25% of the time.
options.semantic_changes: Exact if it implements ABI 4 with d_min windows. In free-running real-time mode (1 model unit about 2.5 us), physical asynchrony replaces simulated jitter and bitwise reproducibility is lost.
options.effort: 12-30 person-weeks after (b2); a small real-time array (tens of cells) on a lab board is the cheaper first step.
options.cost: Same F2 prices. A small development board would also do for a demonstrator (price not verified).
options.risks: Dominant uncertainty: LUTs per processor (1-3k, a 3x swing) and the region size. Growth is limited by the fabric walls. A radius-2 communication gene would multiply wiring 2.5-3x.

options.option: (e) SpiNNaker2 (SpiNNcloud) or Loihi 2 (Intel NRC)
options.speedup_or_benefit: SpiNNaker2 about 110 lives/s per chip (75-157), 0.05x a CPU box. Loihi 2 cannot be estimated without a port and is likely below 1x once the world loop goes through the host. Neither is rentable by the hour. Their benefit is a power-efficient embodied demonstrator, not evolution throughput.
options.semantic_changes: SpiNNaker2: Cortex-M4F cores without double precision, so an integer or float32 model is needed. It can run the event-driven model in C with packet routing, close to the 'cells as cores' picture. Loihi 2: barrier-synchronised time steps (lockstep), microcoded fixed-precision neurons with no sigmoid (needs a piecewise-linear or table substitute), a fixed topology (division needs every site pre-allocated), and the dot world on the embedded cores or the host.
options.effort: SpiNNaker2 8-20 person-weeks, Loihi 2 10-24, plus access negotiation (NRC membership is free for qualified groups).
options.cost: No public hourly price found. Access by application or collaboration.
options.risks: Access and tooling. Model changes, especially Loihi's lockstep and fixed topology. Host I/O per time step could dominate. SpiNNaker2's clock was not verified.

recommendations: For evolution throughput now, keep renting CPUs: a pilot-120 costs about $7 at spot and takes about 2 h on one c7a.48xlarge, or about 0.4 h on five. Add resume/checkpointing first, and merge the exact fast mode (0.5-1 person-week, measured 1.24-1.35x). Custom hardware does not pay back in dollars before about 1,400-18,000 pilots.

Make integer/fixed-point ABI 4 the next model-infrastructure step, because it serves both goals. Use integer timestamps (the ABI already resolves time to 2^-21), Q-format genes, weights and membrane, lookup tables defined in the ABI in place of exp/log/tanh, integer order-free accounting so the accountant's ordered float sums disappear, and a hash cheap in hardware (splitmix64 needs 64x64 multiplies, costly per processor). Gate it on the evolved pilot bodies keeping F within noise. Expected 1.6-2.6x on CPUs (estimate), bitwise portability across machines, and an exact CPU reference for any later FPGA, GPU or ASIC.

Keep the model clockless in the sense that matters: allow hardware clocks and barriers only as event sequencing (integer time) or conservative windows of d_min = 0.5, both of which are exact. Do not adopt lockstep dt as a hidden implementation detail. If time-stepping is wanted for GPU speed, make dt an explicit model parameter, require F at dt and dt/2 to agree within noise, and transfer genomes back to the exact kernel. Keep d_min as a hard floor on every message delay, because that lookahead is what makes exact parallel hardware possible.

Before investing in a GPU, run two cheap measurements, about 1-2 person-weeks and under $20 of compute. First, a CUDA prototype of the cell-step loop with tick queueing on a rented L4 ($0.59/h), to measure the achieved fraction of peak, the dominant GPU uncertainty (6x swing). Second, a CPU time-stepped reference (extend ts_proto.c) to measure how the evolved bodies' F shifts at dt = 0.25, 0.1 and 0.05. Proceed only if F at dt >= 0.05 matches the exact model within noise and the achieved fraction is at least about 0.15.

For the long-term goal of local cell logic in hardware, build the per-cell processor first, not a throughput engine. Write one cell processor (GRN tick, membrane, 8 neighbour ports, lookup tables) in HLS/RTL against the ABI 4 CPU kernel as a bitwise reference, synthesise it to get the real LUT/DSP/memory per processor (the dominant FPGA uncertainty), then run a small real-time array on a lab board. Use AWS F2 ($0.66 spot / $1.98 on-demand per FPGA-hour) only for arrays that need more than one board.

Keep planned model changes hardware-aware. A communication radius of 2 multiplies messages and wiring about 2.5-3x on every platform. Per-channel face weights and gene duplication are bounded arithmetic, about 2x GRN at most. Faster conduction (d0 0.5) halves any time-stepped dt. Where hardware is the destination, prefer the bounded-arithmetic changes over larger neighbourhoods.

Treat neuromorphic chips as a later embodiment target, not an evolution accelerator. SpiNNaker2 (programmable C cores, packet routing, exp/log accelerators) fits the event-driven cell model better than Loihi 2 (microcoded fixed-precision neurons, barrier time steps, fixed topology). Apply to Intel NRC or contact SpiNNcloud only once ABI 4 exists and a real-time demo is wanted. An event camera would map naturally onto the sense plane's receptor events.

Before relying on any rented box, measure its per-core speed with a 10-minute benchmark of the kernel. The 2.0x and 2.6x server-core factors are estimates, and this study measured the unloaded laptop at 1.5-2.9x the audit's loaded baseline.

verdict.title: Skeptic's re-check of the throughput study: the CPU baseline and integer-ABI numbers hold; the GPU and FPGA estimates are about 2x too optimistic; FPGA engines lose per dollar to the integer CPU kernel they depend on

checks.claim: Baseline: pilot-120 is about 768 loaded-laptop CPU-h. One c7a.48xlarge runs about 2,030 lives/s (1,790-2,290), so a pilot takes 2.1 h and costs $7.2 spot / $20.9 on-demand.
checks.recheck: I redid the arithmetic by hand: 15,515,000 lives x 132,000 cell-units x 1.35 us gives 768 h, and 192 x 0.95 / (1.35e-6 x 132,000 / 2.0) gives 2,047 lives/s. I re-fetched the prices (instances.vantage.sh, 2026-10-09): c7a $9.853 on-demand / $3.398 spot, 'AMD EPYC 9R14, up to 3.7 GHz', 1 thread per core; c8a $10.346 / $5.549, 9R45, 1 thread per core. Then I derived my own speed factor for a rented core. I scaled the study's measured P-core figure (0.516 us/cu at 4.99 GHz) to a Zen 4 core at a sustained all-core 3.3-3.7 GHz (estimated), with IPC parity of 0.9-1.15 (estimated). I also added the founder phase (5.8% of pilot wall time, measured in the audit's verdict), which the study leaves out. Script: verify/recheck_model.py.
checks.result: Prices and arithmetic confirmed. My speed factor is 1.86x (1.73-2.0), against the study's 2.0x. That gives 1,890 lives/s (1,760-2,040), 2.4 h (2.2-2.6) including founders, $8.2 spot and $23.7 on-demand per pilot-120 (estimated). This is inside the study's own range, about 10-15% worse. One more point: the real 29-run pilot was about 220 CPU-h (72.3 run-h at 3 threads, audit), not 768. A real pilot therefore costs about $2.3 at spot, so pilot-120 overstates the stakes about 3.5x.

checks.claim: The workload is sparse events plus messaging: per cell-unit 0.50 GRN ticks, 2.6-2.95 packets, 0.017-0.12 spikes and 0.84-1.18 receptor candidates, of which 3.5-4.9% are accepted in SPECK.
checks.recheck: I measured 3 bodies again on my own fresh seeds: BASE = 37,700,000, 6 lives each, T=1100, threads=1, pinned to cpu2. The study used 37,100,000 because the template printed the seed base wrongly. Script: verify/rates.py, output verify/rates_cpu2.json.
checks.result: Confirmed (measured). Ticks 0.500-0.502/cu, packets 2.73-2.83, spikes 0.040 (s0), 0.045 (s5) and 0.128 (v1 s5), candidates 0.96-1.18, acceptance 4.3-4.5% in SPECK and 21% in v1 s5. Speck s5 averages 112.6 cells and speck s0 58. Thread CPU at load average 17, with the P-core's hyperthread sibling busy, was 1.47-1.68 us/cu. That is about 3x the study's light-load 0.52, so laptop timings swing about 3x with load. This supports the study's advice to benchmark the rented box before trusting any speed factor.

checks.claim: An integer/fixed-point ABI 4 kernel would give 1.6-2.6x (mid 2.0x) on CPUs, fast mode included.
checks.recheck: 1) I re-ran the study's bench_ops_base 3 times on E-core cpu5 at load about 17. 2) I did my own Amdahl calculation on the audit's measured profile: arithmetic-type cost centres 48% after the 'ro' change, heap 15%, other 15.5%, scaled to the measured fastro_v3 result of 0.74. I applied 1.6-2.1-3.0x to the arithmetic, 1.0-1.15-1.4x to the heap and 1.0-1.1x to the rest.
checks.result: Confirmed. Microbenchmark (measured): float64 tick 724-747 ns against fixed-point 350-353 ns (2.09x), membrane step 43-46 ns against 12.5-13.9 ns (3.4x), the same as the study. Amdahl (estimated): 2.15x total (p10-p90 1.98-2.32). That is only about 1.6x (1.47-1.72) beyond fast mode, so measured against fast mode the integer ABI breaks even after about 7,300 pilots, not 4,900.

checks.claim: Times are already resolved to 2^-21, so integer time costs nothing semantically, and integer timestamps keep the model exact.
checks.recheck: I read LIFE_ABI.md (world rules, lines 461 and 674) and the time code in kernel.c and spec.py (receptor_next, nextafter).
checks.result: Refuted as stated. 'Resolved to 2^-21 or finer' is a bound on the float64 spacing for |t| <= 2^31, used to guarantee nextup(t) > t. Event times are full-precision doubles: for example receptor_next = t_prev - log(u)/lam with no snapping, and the spacing at t of about 1000 is about 2^-42. Integer time is therefore a real (tiny) quantisation. It creates new exact same-site ties, which the batch rules resolve deterministically. Estimate (birthday bound): at a 2^-21 grid, about 7% of lives would get at least one new same-site coincidence. Statistically negligible, and ABI 4 changes every life anyway, but it is a semantic change, not a free one. The model stays clockless.

checks.claim: A time-stepped GPU gives about 15,600 lives/s per H100 at dt=0.1 (9,500-22,800): 7.7x a c7a box, and 9x per dollar at $2.89/h. L4 gives 3,500-11,200 lives/s, 10-32x per dollar.
checks.recheck: I recomputed the study's point by hand: 541M lane-slots per life, x 0.25 x 33.5e12 gives 15,450 lives/s, so the arithmetic is right. Then I re-fetched the sources (2026-10-09). nvidia.com/h100 gives SXM 67 TFLOPS FP32; the 'PCIe' column now shows H100 NVL at 60 TFLOPS. runpod.io/pricing gives H100 PCIe $1.99 community / $2.89 secure, SXM $2.69 / $3.99, L4 $0.59. The NVIDIA Ada tuning guide gives 100 KB of shared memory per SM on L4, against 228 KB on H100. Then I re-ran the model with these changes. (a) The $2.89 part is a PCIe H100 with 114 SMs at about 1.755 GHz, only 0.77x the SXM issue rate the model credits it with. (b) Shared-memory load/store throughput is 32 lanes/clk/SM, a quarter of the 128-lane issue rate. A cell-step has about 50-65 shared accesses, many of them random neighbour gathers that cause bank conflicts, so I lowered the achieved fraction of peak from 0.08-0.25-0.5 to 0.05-0.15-0.35. (c) A batched tick is a dependent chain of about 1,600 instructions on one lane. I set per-step latency to 2-3-5 us and tick cost to 2,000-3,000-6,000 lane-slots. (d) L4 holds 1-4 resident lives per SM, not 2-8.
checks.result: Corrected (estimated). H100 SXM at dt=0.1: about 8,400 lives/s (5,000-12,500), 4.4x a c7a box (2.6-6.6). Per dollar against c7a spot: 5.6x at $2.69 (community SXM), 3.8x at $3.99 and 2.2x at AWS p5 ($6.88). At dt=0.05: 4,900 lives/s (2.6x a box); at dt=0.25: 13,700 (7.2x). H100 PCIe at dt=0.1: about 6,600. L4 at dt=0.1: about 2,900 lives/s (1,900-4,300), 1.5x a box and about 9x per dollar (5.7-13). Break-even is about 4,400 pilots (unchanged, because the cheaper community price offsets the lower throughput). The semantic cost (lockstep at dt, float32, behaviour depends on dt) is stated correctly in the study and remains the main objection.

checks.claim: FPGA life engines on an AWS F2 VU47P give about 1,000 lives/s (735-1,380): half a c7a box, and 2.5x the CPU's lives per dollar at F2 spot.
checks.recheck: Hand recomputation at the study's mid values: 20.3M cycles per life, 81 ms per life, 84.5 engines, 1,040 lives/s, so the arithmetic is right. I re-fetched f2.6xlarge (vantage, 2026-10-09): $1.98 on-demand, $0.659 spot, 1 FPGA; aws.amazon.com/ec2/instance-types/f2 says VU47P; the F2 HDK README says the shell supplies 250 MHz clk_main_a0 plus 100 MHz, and higher clocks are possible through the AWS clock-generation IP. Then I re-modelled with my own estimates. Engines take 8k-16k-30k LUTs: a 23-knob decode, a derive step with a reciprocal, a priority queue, a hash unit, and the CATCH world/accountant (dot exp, halo, sqrt path, footprint union-find, rare cos/sin/pow) all need room. Events take 6-15-30 cycles, since a first HLS design will stall on read-after-write hazards. DSPs are 2-4-8 per engine. I added the accountant's work per record (about 2.1 records per cell-unit, at 2-8 cycles each), which the study omits. Most importantly, I compared against the integer-ABI CPU kernel, which the engines require (b2 must be built first).
checks.result: Corrected (estimated). About 45 engines, 74 ms per life, about 620 lives/s per VU47P (420-930), 0.33 of a c7a box. Per dollar at F2 spot that is 1.7x the CURRENT CPU kernel, but only 0.78x (0.53-1.2) the integer-ABI CPU kernel on c7a spot, and 0.76x on-demand against on-demand. Against its own prerequisite, then, the FPGA engine never pays back. The study's figure of about 18,000 pilots holds only against the current float kernel (I get about 21,900).

checks.claim: A spatial array with one processor per site runs one life in about 3 ms but gives only about 260 lives/s per FPGA (0.8 of a 508-site body region per chip).
checks.recheck: Recomputed with my own estimate of 2k-4k-8k LUTs per processor. Each site needs a decode unit, a small priority queue for self events, 8 inbound FIFOs, membrane lookup tables and a hash. I also added the serial CATCH accountant: per 0.5-unit window it handles about 60 receptor-candidate thinnings and about 30 tick records in canonical (t, sk, seq) order, at 2-5 cycles each. The study assumes window time equals one processor's tick.
checks.result: Corrected (estimated). 0.34 of a body region per chip, i.e. about 2-4 VU47Ps per body, and about 90 lives/s per FPGA (60-150), 0.05 of a c7a box. The accountant (about 180-600 cycles per window) is as long as the tick and becomes a co-bottleneck. The study's conclusion stands, and more strongly: this design is a demonstrator, not an evolution engine. Thinning would have to be done by per-site world hardware to remove the serial point.

checks.claim: Clock question: conservative windows of width d_min = 0.5 with barriers keep the model exact and clockless. Only lockstep dt-stepping puts the clock into the model. A free-running physical tissue loses only bitwise reproducibility.
checks.recheck: I read LIFE_ABI.md sections 1, 6.1-6.4, 9.7.5 and 11, and the window tests in tests/test_life_time.py.
checks.result: Confirmed for the core claim. Every message (CLAIM, NOTICE, PACKET, ARRIVAL) has delay >= d_min. The world's only feedback, RECEPTOR, lands at t + d_min. Window scheduling with h = 2^-k <= d_min is tested bitwise equal to the heap, including on CATCH bodies, under lockstep ties, and with deaths and refills (test_t1_window_scheduler_equals_heap_on_catch_bodies and others). Two caveats the study glosses over. (1) The accountant is a per-life serial reader of all records in canonical order, so 'local rules only' holds for cells but not for the world machinery in hardware. (2) A free-running tissue loses more than bit-reproducibility: it loses the frozen, place-keyed physics that gives every genome in a generation the same draws (common random numbers). That would make selection noisier, so free-running mode suits embodiment or demos, not evolution.

checks.claim: Break-even against renting CPUs: fast mode about 1,400 pilots, integer ABI about 4,900, time-stepped GPU about 4,700, FPGA engines about 18,000. Nothing pays back at the current scale.
checks.recheck: I recomputed with $3,000 per person-week and the study's mid effort estimates (0.75, 6, 10 and 26 person-weeks), using my corrected per-pilot costs: base $8.18, fast $6.29, integer $3.81, GPU $1.39 (H100 SXM at $2.69), FPGA $4.61.
checks.result: Arithmetic confirmed, and the conclusion is stronger than stated. Fast mode about 1,200 pilots. Integer ABI about 4,100 against base but about 7,300 against fast mode. GPU about 4,400. FPGA about 21,900 against the current kernel and never against the integer kernel it needs. Because a real pilot is about 220 CPU-h ($2.3 spot), every break-even is about 3.5x further away still.

checks.claim: VU47P has about 1,304K LUTs, 9,024 DSPs and 960 URAM blocks (recalled, not verified).
checks.recheck: I tried the AMD product page and the Alveo U55C page (both timed out), the docs.amd.com selection-guide PDF (404, or HTML without the table), and the AWS F2 page (it names the VU47P but gives no resource counts). Web search was unavailable (budget used up).
checks.result: Still unverified. The figures match my own recollection, but no source confirmed them. The FPGA estimates are limited by LUTs per engine or per processor, which are much less certain (2.6-4x swings) than the device totals.

verdict.corrected_summary:
Yes, custom hardware could run the task faster, but at today's scale nothing pays back. The ranking holds; the GPU and FPGA numbers are smaller.

- **Baseline (CPU).** One c7a.48xlarge runs pilot-120 in about 2.4 h (2.2-2.6, founder phase included) for about $8.2 spot or $24 on-demand (estimated, using prices re-fetched 2026-10-09). The real 29-run pilot was about 220 CPU-h, about $2.3 spot.
- **Fast mode.** Measured 1.24-1.35x, about 1,200 pilots to break even.
- **Integer/fixed-point ABI 4.** About 2.15x (2.0-2.3, estimated by Amdahl; microbenchmarks re-measured at 2.09x per tick and 3.4x per membrane step). That is only about 1.6x beyond fast mode. Its value is portability and an exact reference for any hardware build. One caveat: event times are full float64 today, so integer time is a small quantisation, not a free change.
- **Time-stepped GPU.** H100 SXM about 8,400 lives/s at dt=0.1 (5,000-12,500), about 4.4x a c7a box and 3.8-5.6x per dollar at $2.69-3.99/h (2.2x at AWS p5). L4 about 2,900 lives/s, about 9x per dollar. This holds only if lockstep dt becomes part of the model and is validated.
- **FPGA life engines.** About 620 lives/s per VU47P (420-930), about 0.33 of a CPU box. That is 1.7x the current kernel per dollar at F2 spot, but 0.78x the integer CPU kernel the engines require, so they never pay back.
- **Spatial array (one processor per site).** About 90 lives/s per FPGA, with 2-4 FPGAs per body plus a serial accountant bottleneck. Useful as a demonstrator only.
- **Neuromorphic chips.** Unchanged: not an evolution accelerator.
- **Clocks.** Exact and clockless as long as every message keeps delay >= d_min and the machine uses conservative d_min windows. Lockstep dt (GPU, Loihi 2) puts a clock into the model. Free-running hardware also loses the shared per-generation physics draws that evolution uses for fair comparisons between genomes.

Recommendations unchanged: rent CPUs, merge fast mode, build integer ABI 4 with a hardware-cheap hash, then synthesise one per-cell processor against it.
verdict.missed:
1. The study compares FPGA engines with the current float kernel. They require ABI 4, and against the integer CPU kernel they lose per dollar (about 0.8x), so they never break even.
2. GPU limits it omits: shared-memory load/store runs at 32 lanes/clk/SM, a quarter of issue width, and random neighbour gathers cause bank conflicts. A batched GRN tick is a long dependent chain that limits latency per step. L4 has 100 KB of shared memory per SM (NVIDIA Ada tuning guide, fetched 2026-10-09), so it holds fewer lives than H100. The $2.89 RunPod price is for a 114-SM PCIe part, about 0.77x the SXM throughput the model credits it with.
3. The CATCH accountant is serial per life: about 2 records per cell-unit, mostly receptor thinning, sorted by (t, sk, seq). The spatial-array model and the engine cycle counts both leave this cost out.
4. Integer time is a quantisation. Today's event times are full float64, not on a 2^-21 grid.
5. The founder phase (5.8% of pilot wall time) is left out of the workload.
6. The real pilot was about 220 CPU-h, not 768, so dollars per pilot and every break-even are about 3.5x more favourable to plain CPUs than stated.
7. Bitwise portability across machines also needs the evolution loop's torch mutation RNG pinned (ATEN_CPU_CAPABILITY, flagged by the audit). ABI 4 alone does not provide it.
8. On FPGA, splitmix64 needs 64x64 multiplies, about 16-20 DSPs per pipelined hash unit at about 16 hash rounds per cell-unit. This supports the study's call for a cheaper hash, but the engine LUT/DSP budget omits it.
9. Engine LUTs per life engine are probably larger than 6-16k once the 23-knob decode, the reciprocal in derive, the priority queue and the world unit (footprint union-find, cos/sin/pow) are included. A first HLS design will also spend more than 8 cycles per event.
10. Free-running physical tissue loses the place-keyed shared random draws that evolution uses to compare genomes fairly, so it fits embodiment or demos, not selection.
11. VU47P resource totals and the SpiNNaker2 clock remain unverified (AMD pages timed out or returned 404; the arXiv paper states no clock).

report.title: Co-designing the cell model for hardware: a hardware-native ABI does not change how the evolved bodies behave

findings.claim:
These rules are hardware-hostile. Each has a hardware-native equivalent that keeps behaviour:
(a) float64 with libm exp/log/tanh: fixed point plus tables defined by the ABI. That means an exp2 unit (Q8 exponent, 256-entry Q16 table, then a shift), a 256-entry log2 table and a 256-entry Q12 sigmoid table on [-8, 8). q8(2 tanh y) is exactly 15 comparator thresholds, so pol needs no table.
(b) Exact exponential membrane decay and the log threshold prediction: an integer step count times a per-cell Q16 rate kappa = h log2(e) / tau, fed to the exp2 unit. The crossing step comes from the log2 table and is rounded up.
(c) Poisson receptor candidates (log draws) thinned by the world: one Bernoulli(lambda h) trial per step, against a per-cell rate the world supplies, like a pixel.
(d) The dense 16x25 + 23x16 GRN: an integer MAC engine shared over time, which skips zero weights.
(e) Knob decodes: TAU_M, t_ref, p = 2^(k-8), delta, kappa and phi are already table or shift operations. asym and sec use the sigmoid table; Dm and km are decoded once per genome.
(f) The morphogen max-normalisation (a division per tick): a reciprocal table with shat in Q8, or no division at all once face weights replace a_c*shat.
(g) m/(1+m): a reciprocal table.
(h) splitmix64 folding: per-site CRC digests for verification, and a 32-bit counter-based hash keyed by (site, birth index, counter) for draws.
(i) Per-event records and the canonical-order float accountant: per-cell integer counters, which sum in any order, plus a narrow motor/stroke stream to the world.
(j) The heap: per-site timer registers (tick, threshold, receptor) plus per-slot arrival FIFOs. Delays are bounded at about 4 units.
(k) The sorted inbox: per-cell integer mass accumulators plus the latest concentration per slot.
(l) The unbounded fabric and 64-bit uids: a fixed site array whose edges are walls.
findings.evidence:
- CPU shares (measured earlier in compute_audit.json, not re-measured here): libm 19%, heap 14-16%, hash folding about 10%, records, sort and accountant about 13%. Receptor candidates are 43-60% of heap events, and about 4% are accepted in SPECK.
- Table errors (measured, hw_primitives.py, pure integers): decay abs error ≤ 0.0019, ln ≤ 0.0019, sigmoid ≤ 0.0079. The tables total 11.5 kbit.
- Swapping (a), (b), (d)-(g) into the kernel copy (variant 'arith': exp/log tables, sigmoid table, Q12 genes and inputs, Q16 morphogen, Q8 shat): pooled dF +0.004 ± 0.040 over 6 bodies; worst body s6 −0.22 ± 0.12 (z −1.9). 512 paired lives per body, seed0 37,300,000.
- The structural items (h)-(l) are design reasoning from LIFE_ABI.md sections 6-11 and were not prototyped.

findings.claim: The full hardware-native candidate is behaviour-neutral on the evolved bodies. It combines tables, Q16 genes, Q16 chemistry, integer time h = 1/64 with unbiased rounding, and the genome on a 1/64 grid (W, b) and a 1/128 grid (A, a0). It is not bitwise: every life diverges, so a hardware ABI must be its own reference.

findings.claim: Genome precision trap: readout weights A and a0 on a 1/32 grid change development, while a 1/128 grid is neutral. W and b tolerate 1/16. The likely reason is that knob decodes are thresholds (rint(4y), L(y), q8), so readout error moves division and placement decisions.
findings.evidence:
Measured (512 paired lives per body):
- A, a0 on 1/32 (wqA): s6 −0.56 ± 0.12 (z −4.9); final size s4 −10.3, s6 −9.4, s8 −8.4 cells, s2 +13.2.
- All fields coarse (wq: W 1/16, A 1/32): s6 −0.63 ± 0.11, and s6's full hardware set with it −0.90 ± 0.12.
- W, b on 1/16 alone (wqW): +0.04 ± 0.08 (2 bodies).
- W 1/64, A 1/128 (wqfine): pooled +0.07 ± 0.04, worst body +0.002, sizes within ±1.6 cells.
- The evolved genomes reach |W| up to 23.7 (the n_view prior std 8) and |A| up to 3.3 (raw_genome_stats.json). So W fits int12 (1/64 step, ±32) and A fits int11 (1/128 step, ±8).

The threshold mechanism is inferred, not tested.

findings.claim: Integer time works without a central clock if rounding is unbiased and the grid is fine (about 32 steps per d_min). Rounding every interval up lowers event rates. Coarse grids change behaviour even when unbiased.
findings.evidence:
Measured, naive ceil rounding of every event time, pooled dF over 6 bodies:
- h 1/64: −0.00 ± 0.04
- h 1/16: −0.08 ± 0.04
- h 1/4: −0.67 ± 0.04, with spikes −20 to −31% (smoke, s5: receptor candidates 110.5k → 83.1k)

Cause: rounding a Poisson interval up lowers the rate by about lambda h / 2 (1.6%, 6% and 26% at lambda 2.05).

Measured, unbiased rounding (delays and tick periods to the nearest step, receptor = a Bernoulli(lambda h) trial per step, crossings rounded up):
- 1/64: +0.06 ± 0.04
- 1/16: +0.02 ± 0.05
- 1/4: +0.20 ± 0.04 (s5 +0.47, z 3.5; s4 +0.28; 4 of 6 bodies up)

Control (measured): float with jit = 0 and delay_sd = 0 gives +0.02 ± 0.06 (3 bodies), so removing delay jitter does not explain the 1/4 effect. Its cause is unknown, so a 1/4 grid is not neutral.

At 1/64, jitter of ±0.1 spans about 13 steps and d_min 0.25 still spans 16 steps.

findings.claim: Genes need 16 fractional bits, not 12. At Q12 a slow gene stops changing once its update step rounds to zero, short of its target.
findings.evidence:
- Measured (integer simulation, hw_primitives.json): a Q12 gene stops 1.5% from its target at lambda 2^-7 and 0.76% at 2^-6. At Q16: 0.10% and 0.05%.
- On the evolved bodies the difference is invisible: gq (Q12) pooled +0.007 ± 0.041, gq16 +0.014 ± 0.024 (5 bodies, measured).
- The hand-built lineage timer (lambda 1/128) would be affected; this is inferred from its design.

findings.claim: Evolving directly in the hardware ABI should start from the same founder landscape, so a loss of expressivity is unlikely. This rests on transplants and a founder census; no evolution was run.
findings.evidence:
Measured, census_hw.py: 8,192 random SPECK founders (founder sampling of configs/life_speck.yaml, generator seed 37,300,123), one life each on the same seeds (37,500,000+i), float64 against the full hardware set:
- earners: 217 vs 228
- F ≥ 0: 36 vs 37 (0.44% vs 0.45%)
- guard trips: 2,305 vs 2,315
- lone cells: 4,351 vs 4,354
- Spearman of F: 0.993 over all genomes, 0.987 over earners

The transplant results (finding 2) show that the evolved mechanisms (voting, coincidence detection, feedback inhibition, crowding gain, gradient-made directional synapses) are all expressible in the hardware arithmetic.

findings.claim: Prices set from hardware energy would barely change selection today. The tick rate is fixed and every best has about the same multiply-accumulates and packets per tick, so c_live already acts as a GRN-tick price. Hardware prices matter only once tick rate, active genes or sparsity, chemistry use or radius can evolve.
findings.evidence:
Re-pricing (measured lives, estimated energies): c_live, c_spike and c_msg were replaced by kappa x energy, normalised to the same mean compute cost.
- F changes by at most 0.014 / 0.018 / 0.033 (low/mid/high energies).
- Rank correlation of the 11 bodies: 1.00 / 0.99 / 0.99.

Today's compute prices give 92-99% to c_live and 1-8% to spikes plus contacts (measured).

Implied prices at mid energies (model cost units), against today:
- GRN tick: 0.033 sparse / 0.059 dense; today c_live 0.02 per unit at 0.5 ticks per unit = 0.04 per tick
- packet: 0.0008; unpriced today
- spike base: 0.0011; today c_spike 0.004
- contact send plus arrival: 0.0014; today c_msg 0.001
- receptor candidate: 0.00027; unpriced today

findings.claim: A hardware clock is acceptable as an implementation detail. Fully clockless hardware is possible with only local handshakes.
findings.evidence:
Contract reasoning (LIFE_ABI.md 6.3 and 11.2):
- Every cross-site effect takes at least d_min, and the window scheduler (windows h ≤ d_min) is already bitwise equal to the heap scheduler.
- So a synchronous step machine with h ≤ d_min, on integer times, implements the same semantics.
- Cells never read the step index. Their own clocks stay per-cell jittered integer periods (P0 2 = 128 ± 13 steps), so nothing runs in lockstep.

Sourced (Loihi paper, fetched 2026-10-09): Loihi is asynchronous bundled-data digital logic. It still advances a fixed algorithmic time step by a mesh-wide barrier of 113-465 ns over 1-32 tiles. The paper notes these steps 'relate to the algorithmic time of the computation and need not have a direct relationship to the hardware execution time'.

Our d_min floor is the lookahead of conservative parallel discrete-event simulation (reasoning). A site may advance once its neighbours promise nothing before t + d_min, which allows up to 32 steps of skew at h 1/64 with no global barrier.

In physical-time hardware, the per-cell free-running oscillators would be the model's clock_sd and tick_jit (reasoning).

- Faster conduction under the hardware set: measured +0.013 ± 0.045 against float.
- Radius 2 raises in-plane contacts from 6 to 18 (review L7). Per-site slot state and spike fan-out rise by about 2.25-3x (estimated), and hop energy scales with wire length (Loihi tile hop 3-4 pJ, sourced).
- Gene count sets multiply-accumulates per tick (25 per active row plus 23 readout per active column), so duplication raises GRN energy about linearly (estimated).
- Mutation is Gaussian on random entries (src/genome.py:448), so exact zeros never evolve. Sparsity-aware hardware would need gene deletion or a per-weight enable bit.

findings.claim: Hardware sizing, rough estimate: about 2 kbit of state per site and about 8-10 kbit of genome shared per body. A 1,024-site array needs about 2 Mbit of on-chip SRAM. A pipelined FPGA life engine might run a SPECK life in 5-20 ms.

options.option: A. Change nothing now: keep evolving in float64 (ABI 3, then ABI 4) and translate the evolved genomes to hardware later
options.speedup_or_benefit: No speedup now. A later translation would mostly work: measured +0.04 ± 0.04 F on transplanted bests with a fine genome grid. Every translated body still needs a statistical check and possibly retuning; a coarse readout grid shrank bodies by 5-10 cells and cost s6 0.56 F.
options.semantic_changes: None now.
options.effort: 0 now; later 1-3 person-weeks to translate and re-validate.
options.risks:
- New mechanisms get designed in hardware-hostile forms (divisions, unbounded inbox, 64-bit uids, libm).
- Bitwise reproducibility across machines stays tied to glibc's FMA path (found in the compute audit).
- The pilot's results cannot be replayed on hardware.

options.option: B. Hardware-native ABI (recommended): build the planned ABI-4 cleanup on an integer base, with a CPU integer kernel and an integer reference that future RTL must match bit for bit. Uses integer time h = 2^-6 with unbiased rounding, ABI-defined exp2/log2/sigmoid tables, Q16 genes and morphogens, the genome on integer grids and an integer ledger.
options.speedup_or_benefit:
- CPU speed: estimated 1.2-1.6x per core, the same per dollar and per wall-hour. Basis: tables replace libm (19% of CPU); integer sums make the canonical record sort and float accountant (about 13%) unnecessary; hash folds (9.3%) are already removable in fast mode. My prototype emulates the tables with libm, so its timings say nothing.
- Main benefits: bitwise portability across CPUs, glibc versions and ARM; an executable specification for RTL; an exact integer ledger.
- Behaviour: measured dF +0.04 ± 0.04 on 6 bests; founder landscape Spearman 0.993.
options.semantic_changes:
- Time in steps of 1/64: crossings land on the next step, receptor events are one Bernoulli(lambda h) trial per step, and exact coincidences are possible but rare.
- Tables replace libm: abs error ≤ 0.002 for exp and log, ≤ 0.008 for sigmoid.
- Genes and morphogens are 16-bit fractions; the genome lies on fixed grids (W, b 1/64 within ±32; A, a0 1/128 within ±8).
- One life per genome, local rules, genome-driven division and death, and no central clock in the model are all unchanged.
options.effort: 4-8 person-weeks: the integer C kernel, an integer Python mirror (or the frozen float reference as a statistical oracle), tests, re-baselined gates and goldens. Skills: C fixed-point numerics and the ABI contract. Cheapest if merged with the ABI-4 cleanup (X2), which changes every life anyway.
options.cost: A few CPU-hours of validation lives (under $1 rented).
options.risks:
- Every golden changes, and pilot results are only statistically comparable.
- Overflow and saturation rules must be written down.
- Coarse grids are not neutral, so the grid must stay at about 1/64.
- Two ABIs coexist during the transition.

options.option: C. FPGA life engine (simulation accelerator for evolution) implementing the hardware ABI
options.speedup_or_benefit:
- Per engine (estimated): 5-20 ms per SPECK life, against 70-150 ms per laptop E-core (measured) or about 35-75 ms per server core (estimated).
- Per FPGA (estimated): 16-64 engines, about 40-600 core-equivalents.
- Prices (sourced): f2.6xlarge with one VU47P costs $1.98/h on demand, $0.659/h spot; c7a.48xlarge with 192 cores costs $9.85/h on demand, $3.40/h spot (prices from the compute audit).
- So an estimated 1-15x better per dollar than CPU, and per wall-hour one FPGA is worth about 0.2-3 of the 192-core boxes.
- A pilot already costs $6-16 on CPUs, so the saving is a few dollars per pilot. It pays only for campaigns of more than about 10^4 CPU-hours.
options.semantic_changes: None beyond option B, if the RTL matches the integer reference bitwise. That is verified by per-site CRC event digests on random lives.
options.effort: 3-6 person-months after option B: RTL or HLS of the site processor, GRN engine and timing wheel; Verilator co-simulation; AWS FPGA HDK; a host loop for the world engine and evolution. Skills: HDL, verification, FPGA tooling.
options.cost: F2 spot about $0.66/h during development and runs. Not verified: whether Vivado licensing on the F2 developer AMI is included.
options.risks:
- Development cost outweighs the compute saved at the current scale.
- The world engine (dot, blobs, receptor rates) on the host may become the bottleneck.
- Every model change (face weights, radius gene, energy store) needs new RTL, so the ABI must be frozen first.

options.option: D. Neuromorphic chips (Loihi 2 through INRC, SpiNNaker2)
options.speedup_or_benefit:
Unknown, probably none for evolution throughput.
- Loihi (sourced): synaptic op 23.6 pJ, neuron update 52-81 pJ (Loihi 1, 14 nm).
- Our per-cell GRN (about 350 multiply-accumulates per tick) and growth do not map onto native neurons.
- SpiNNaker2 runs C on ARM cores, so it is roughly a low-power many-core CPU.
options.semantic_changes:
- Loihi's barrier-synchronised algorithmic time step fits integer time.
- Loihi 1 weights are limited to 1-9 bits (sourced, Davies 2018).
- Growth needs pre-allocated compartments.
- Exactness holds only against a chip-specific reference.
options.effort: 2-4 person-months, plus access. Per the sibling platform agent's sources, Lava was archived on 2026-05-13 (github.com/lava-nc/lava); not re-checked by me.
options.cost: INRC access is free for qualified groups (sibling agent's source, intel.com); no purchase price.
options.risks:
- Dynamic topology and the per-cell GRN are not native.
- The SDK is changing.
- Availability is limited.
- Not a deployment path we control.

options.option: E. Custom digital ASIC: a cellular array that runs in physical time (the Embryonics-like deployment target)
options.speedup_or_benefit:
- Energy (estimated): 0.3-1.6 nJ per cell per model time unit.
- At 1 µs per model unit, a 1,000-cell tissue draws about 0.3-1.6 W.
- At robot speed (1 ms per unit), dynamic power is about 0.3-1.6 mW per 1,000 cells, and leakage dominates. Leakage is about 25 µW per cell for about 0.25 KB of state at 100 mW/MB (sourced rate, estimated state size). Bits of state per cell then become the main cost.
options.semantic_changes:
- Physical time.
- Can be clockless (asynchronous logic, per-cell oscillators standing in for clock_sd and tick_jit).
- Deterministic if digital.
- Replay needs logged inputs.
options.effort: 6-18 person-months to a first multi-cell test chip. One hardware-ABI cell (MAC engine, 3 tables, about 2 kbit of state) is estimated at 20-50k gates.
options.cost: Prototype shuttles (sibling platform agent's sources, fetched 2026-10-09): Tiny Tapeout EUR 70 per tile of about 1,000 gates; ChipFoundry chipIgnite $14,950 per tapeout with up to 15 mm2 in SKY130.
options.risks:
- Very long feedback loop.
- The ABI must be frozen first.
- Real sensors and actuators must be built.
- Fab delivery takes 6-12 months.

options.option: F. Analog or mixed-signal continuous time (BrainScaleS-2 style)
options.speedup_or_benefit:
- Truly clockless, with physical exponential decay for free and about 1000x biological speed.
- An evolution loop of 200 generations x 1,000 individuals ran in about 12 h (sibling agent's source, arXiv 2201.11063).
options.semantic_changes:
- No bitwise reproducibility.
- Device mismatch and noise replace the frozen tau_mis and clock_sd.
- The GRN would run on embedded processors.
- Forks by replay become statistical.
options.effort: Research-level, 6-12+ person-months. Access route (EBRAINS) not verified.
options.cost: Access-based; unknown.
options.risks:
- Loses exact replay and forks, which the project's analyses rely on.
- Behaviour must be evolved under noise.
- Hard to match the reference model.

recommendations: Make the GRN tick a numerical step, not biology: use per-time gene and fate laws (X2a/b) on the same exp2 unit. Hardware can then pick its tick rate, the energy-dominant knob at 65-87% (estimated). Keep P0 2 until the P0 4 arm (L5) is measured.

Do not save hardware steps with a coarse time grid. At 1/16 and 1/4 the grid changed behaviour: −0.08 F with naive rounding at 1/16, and +0.20 F, unexplained, at 1/4 even with unbiased rounding. Keep about 32 steps per d_min.

Prices: do not switch to hardware-energy prices now; re-pricing the 11 bests changed F by at most 0.03 and left the ranking unchanged. Add a post-hoc hardware-energy panel to the analysis. It needs no kernel change: ticks x the genome's nonzero multiply-accumulates, packets, contact events, arrivals, receptor candidates and cell-time are all in the ledger. Introduce per-tick, per-multiply-accumulate, per-packet or per-hop prices only together with the change that makes that quantity evolvable (per-cell tick period L5, duplication X3, radius L7). Make them a split of c_live that keeps the total calibrated (the review showed the price level moves the router's lead), test them as an A/B arm, and keep c_tw, c_div and c_miss as biology/world prices. Expected effects (inferred): sparser, smaller GRNs, slower gene clocks in quiet cells, less chemistry, and relatively cheaper spike-based computation.

Next stage: the integer CPU kernel and an integer Python mirror, checked bitwise against each other on random lives and goldens, and statistically against the float ABI by the gate above. Then run a 3-seed SPECK A/B, hardware ABI against float at matched generations. That is the real expressivity test; this study only shows transplants and founders are unchanged.

Later stage:
- RTL of one site processor plus GRN engine under Verilator, cross-checked against the integer reference by per-site CRC digests of the event stream on thousands of random lives.
- An FPGA life engine (for example AWS F2 spot at $0.66/h) only when campaigns exceed about 10^4 CPU-hours.
- Long term, a physical-time ASIC cellular array. There leakage makes per-cell state bits the dominant price, so keep per-cell state small (genes, slots, FIFOs).
