verdict.title: Re-check of "codesign": the hardware-native arithmetic holds up, but an FPGA simulator does not pay off and two clock claims overreach

checks.claim: The full hardware candidate (hw64u_fine: lookup tables, Q16 genes and chemistry, time step h = 1/64 with unbiased rounding, W on a 1/64 grid, A on a 1/128 grid) does not change how the evolved bodies behave: pooled dF +0.044 ± 0.040 over 6 bodies, worst −0.10, and final sizes move by −0.3 to +1.5 cells.
checks.recheck:
1. Read hw_patch.py, hw_run.py and kernel_hw.c to see what the prototype actually changes.
2. Reran float 'base' against hw64u_fine with the study's own builds, on NEW seeds: fresh_seeds(1024, seed0=37,800,000).
3. Used all 11 pilot bests: the study's 6, plus SPECK s0, s1, s3, s7 and s9, which it never tested.
4. Paired the lives by seed.
Files: verify/replicate.py, verify/rep_analyse.py, verify/rep.jsonl, verify/rep_summary.json.
checks.result:
Measured, F:
- Pooled over 11 bodies: −0.012 ± 0.020. On the study's 6 bodies: −0.019 ± 0.029. On the 5 new bodies: −0.005 ± 0.028.
- Per body from −0.12 (s1, z −2.0) to +0.13 (s3, z +2.6). Chi-square of the 11 z values is 12.6 on 11 degrees of freedom, which is consistent with no effect.
- The study's largest per-body values (s2 +0.18, s8 +0.17) were noise. On new seeds they are +0.015 and −0.03.

Measured, development: it does shift, by small but real amounts.
- Final size: s9 −4.2 ± 0.8, s3 +3.9 ± 0.5, s1 −1.9 ± 0.5, s8 +1.9 ± 0.2, s7 −1.3 ± 0.1 cells. 7 of 11 bodies have |z| > 3.
- Spike counts move by −4% to +4%. No life keeps its hash.

Not actually tested: the prototype is the float64 kernel with rounding inserted at chosen points. These stay float64:
- traces, twitch, the decay-exponent divisions (t − t0)/tau, m/(1+m), the trace/tau inputs before rounding, and all of the world physics.
- The receptor is not one Bernoulli trial per step. It is a geometric skip drawn with a log table, then the accountant's float thinning.
- The fixed site array with walls, the 32-bit hash keyed by site and birth index, bounded arrival FIFOs and the integer ledger were never built.
So 'replaced float64 and libm with fixed-point state' overstates what was run.

checks.claim: Genome precision trap: readout weights A and a0 on a 1/32 grid change development (s6 −0.56 F, bodies 8-10 cells smaller), while a 1/128 grid is neutral.
checks.recheck: Reran wqA (A and a0 on 1/32) against base on speck_s4, s6 and s8 with my new seeds (1024 lives each).
checks.result:
Measured:
- s6: −0.59 ± 0.09 F (z −6.9). The study had −0.56.
- s4: −0.15 ± 0.07.
- s8: −0.04 ± 0.07.
- Final size −10.8, −9.8 and −7.5 cells (study: −10.3, −9.4, −8.4). Spikes −7% to −19%.
The 1/128 grid passes the F check above. The explanation through decode thresholds is still untested.

checks.claim: Integer time needs a fine grid and unbiased rounding. Rounding every interval up at h = 1/4 costs 0.67 F (a rate loss of about lambda h / 2, so 26% at h = 1/4). Even unbiased, a 1/4 grid is not neutral: +0.20 ± 0.04, cause unknown.
checks.recheck:
1. Recomputed the exact rate loss from always rounding up: mean interval h / (1 − e^(−λh)), at λ = 2.05.
2. Reran t4u (h = 1/4, unbiased) against base on all 11 bodies with new seeds (1024 lives each).
3. Rechecked the Q12/Q16 gene-stall arithmetic.
checks.result:
- Rate loss, exact: 1.6%, 6.1% and 21.8% at h = 1/64, 1/16 and 1/4. The λh/2 rule gives 1.6%, 6.4% and 25.6%, so it overstates the loss at 1/4.
- t4u, measured: pooled +0.107 ± 0.021 over 11 bodies (z ≈ 5). On the study's 6: +0.133 ± 0.030. Spikes +2% to +12%; sizes −4.1 to +5.2 cells.
- So the conclusion that 1/4 is not neutral replicates, at about half the size.
- Which bodies move does not replicate: the study had s5 +0.47 and s6 +0.03; I get s5 +0.11 and s6 +0.29.
- Gene stall: the gap is 2^−(q+1)/lambda, which gives 1.56% (Q12) and 0.098% (Q16) at lambda 2^−7. That matches the study.

checks.claim: Founder census: 8,192 random SPECK founders rank almost the same in float and in hardware arithmetic (Spearman 0.993; 36 against 37 founders with F ≥ 0), so evolving inside the hardware ABI should start from the same landscape.
checks.recheck:
1. Repeated the census on new founders (generator seed 37,800,123).
2. Added a noise floor: the same founders in float on a second, different set of seeds. The study had no such floor.
Files: verify/census_null.py, verify/census_null.json, verify/census_{fA,fB,hA}.npz.
checks.result:
Measured:
- Float against hardware on the same seeds: Spearman 0.993 (0.984 over earners). 136 of 258 earners earn in both; 21 of 37 F ≥ 0 founders are F ≥ 0 in both. F ≥ 0 counts 27 against 31; earners 194 against 200.
- Float against float on different seeds: Spearman 0.953 (0.899 over earners). Only 55 of 355 earners earn in both, and 5 of 62 F ≥ 0 founders.
Switching to the hardware arithmetic perturbs a founder's life much less than redrawing its life seed. That makes the claim stronger than the study argued. Still, a founder census is not an evolution run.

checks.claim: An FPGA life engine runs a SPECK life in 5-20 ms. With 16-64 engines per VU47P it is 1-15x better per dollar than CPUs, and it pays off for campaigns above about 10^4 CPU-hours.
checks.recheck:
1. Built my own cycle model from measured per-life counts (energy_counts.json; mean of 11 bests: 44k ticks, 243k packets, 93k receptor candidates, 19k arrivals).
2. Ran three engine designs at 200 and 250 MHz.
3. Redid the price and break-even arithmetic.
4. Re-fetched sources on 2026-10-09:
- vantage.sh f2.6xlarge: $1.980/h on demand, $0.659/h spot, 24 vCPU, 1 FPGA. The region is not stated.
- aws.amazon.com/ec2/instance-types/f2/: VU47P with 16 GB HBM; f2.6xlarge has 24 vCPU and 64 GB DDR4.
- AWS F2 HDK docs (awsdocs-fpga-f2.readthedocs-hosted.com): the small shell leaves 88% of resources for user logic, with a 250 MHz main clock.
Files: verify/fpga_model.py, verify/fpga_model.txt.
checks.result:
Estimated:
- Engine time per life: 9-21 ms with perfect overlap or a well-pipelined dense GRN; 43-70 ms for a first HLS design that does not overlap the non-multiply work of each tick. The study's 5-20 ms assumes 16 MAC lanes kept fully busy.
- Per dollar against 192-core CPU spot ($0.0177 per core-hour): 0.4-2.8x at 50 ms per life, 1.4-9.5x at 15 ms, 4-28x only at 5 ms with 16-48 engines.

The world has to be in RTL, not on the host (missed by the study):
- The host must thin about 93k receptor candidates per life, each with a float halo exp.
- At 32 engines and 10 ms per life (3,200 lives/s), that needs about 15-30 host cores. f2.6xlarge has 24 vCPU, about 12 physical cores.
- Each receptor needs a round trip within d_min of model time.

Break-even is wrong by at least 100x:
- 10^4 CPU-hours cost only $177 (spot) to $513 (on demand) on CPUs.
- If 3-6 person-months of development are valued at $30-90k, break-even is about 2-10 million CPU-hours, or roughly 8,000-46,000 pilots of 220 CPU-hours.

Not verified: VU47P LUT, BRAM, URAM and DSP counts (amd.com timed out repeatedly), and Vivado licensing on F2.

checks.claim: A hardware clock is fine as an implementation detail. Fully clockless hardware needs only neighbour-to-neighbour handshakes, not a global barrier. A physical-time digital ASIC (option E) can be clockless and is 'deterministic if digital'. Exact coincidences under integer time are 'possible but rare'.
checks.recheck:
1. Read LIFE_ABI.md sections 1, 2, 6.2-6.4, 7.10, 9.1, 9.7.5 and 11.
2. Read the Loihi paper text the study saved: Table 2 and the barrier section.
3. Estimated same-site coincidences from the measured event rate: about 1.7 heap events per cell-unit.
checks.result:
Confirmed:
- A synchronous clock that processes logical-time events in windows h ≤ d_min is exactly the contract's window scheduler (11.2). Cells cannot see it.
- The Loihi figures are confirmed: 23.6 pJ per synaptic op, 81/52 pJ per neuron update, 1.7 pJ within a tile, 3.0/4.0 pJ per tile hop, 113-465 ns mesh-wide barrier. So is the 'need not have a direct relationship' quote.

Corrected:
- In CATCH and SPECK the world/accountant is a hub. It reads every act-plane spike record in canonical order and sends RECEPTOR events to every sense cell at t + d_min. A distributed simulator therefore needs a world-wide synchronisation at least every d_min. Only the tissue is neighbour-local.
- Guards and extinction checks are global counts too, but they only end a life, so they can be checked lazily.
- Option E cannot be both clockless with free-running per-cell oscillators and deterministic. Arbitration between near-simultaneous inputs then depends on analog timing, so exact replay and forks are lost, much as with analog hardware. Determinism requires logical-time (timestamped) hardware.
- Coincidences: about 2-5% of events at a site share a 1/64 step (estimate). That is thousands of merged batches per life, not 'rare'. The batch rule (6.2) defines how they are handled, but the coincidence window becomes 1/64 wide.

checks.claim: Estimated hardware energy is 0.3-1.6 nJ per cell per model time unit, with GRN ticks at 65-87%. Re-pricing the 11 bests by hardware energy changes F by at most 0.03 and keeps their ranking. LLC leakage is about 100 mW/MB (Horowitz).
checks.recheck:
1. Read energy_model.py and its output.
2. Recomputed the shares, the per-tick prices and the maximum |dF|.
3. Checked the Horowitz PDF text the study saved.
checks.result:
- Arithmetic: matches the output. Mid prices are 0.0332 per sparse tick and 0.0587 per dense tick. Maximum |dF| is 0.014, 0.018 and 0.033 at low, mid and high energies; rank correlation is 1.00, 0.99 and 0.99.
- Horowitz text, confirmed: 'We estimate the leakage to be around 100mW/MB'. This is an LLC estimate that depends on technology.
- The 768-MAC 'dense' figure assumes all 16 genes. The bests have about 8 active genes, so a dense engine over active genes needs about 384 MACs.
- The result is internally consistent. Every per-operation energy is an estimate.

checks.claim: Minor primitives: q8(2 tanh y) is 15 comparator thresholds. An integer CPU kernel would be 1.2-1.6x faster per core.
checks.recheck:
1. Enumerated q8(2 tanh y) on a fine grid of y.
2. Re-read the compute audit's fast-mode figures.
checks.result:
- q8(2 tanh y) has 33 levels, which takes 32 thresholds (16 per sign), not 15. Still no table is needed.
- The 1.2-1.6x includes hash-fold removal, which today's exact fast mode already gives (1.24-1.35x) with no ABI change.
- The CATCH world still needs records in canonical order, so the accountant's share does not all disappear.
- The speedup the hardware ABI adds on top of fast mode is probably about 1.1-1.3x (estimate; nothing timed).

verdict.corrected_summary:
Faster on an FPGA? Not in any way that pays off. Building toward hardware-friendly cell logic now? Yes. The cheap step is the integer, hardware-native ABI.

**What holds (measured on new seeds 37,800,000+, 1024 paired lives per body, all 11 pilot bests):**
- The hardware arithmetic does not change fitness: pooled dF −0.012 ± 0.020, per body −0.12 to +0.13.
- The arithmetic was a float64 kernel with fixed-point rounding at selected points (tables, Q16 genes and morphogens, 1/64 time with unbiased rounding, W on a 1/64 grid, A on a 1/128 grid).
- It does change development a little: final size moves by −4.2 to +3.9 cells, significant in 7 of 11 bodies, and spikes by ±4%. So it is fitness-neutral, not behaviour-identical.
- The readout-grid trap replicates. A and a0 on 1/32 cost s6 0.59 F and shrink bodies by 7.5-10.8 cells, so 1/128 is needed.
- A 1/4 time grid is not neutral even with unbiased rounding (+0.11 ± 0.02 F), so keep about 1/64.
- In a founder census, the hardware arithmetic perturbs a life far less than redrawing its seed: Spearman 0.993 against 0.953; 136 of 258 earners keep earning under the hardware arithmetic, against 55 of 355 under a new seed. Evolving directly in the hardware ABI is therefore unlikely to lose expressivity, though no evolution was run.
- A hardware clock is fine as an implementation detail. A synchronous machine processing logical-time windows h ≤ d_min is the contract's own window scheduler.

**Corrections:**
- **Prototype scope.** It was not a fixed-point kernel. Traces, twitch, the decay divisions and the whole world stay float64. The site walls, 32-bit hashes, bounded FIFOs, integer ledger and per-step receptor were never built. The real integer kernel still has to pass the same tests.
- **FPGA speed** (estimated):
  - 9-21 ms per life for a well-pipelined engine, 43-70 ms for a first HLS design. A server core takes about 35-110 ms.
  - Per dollar, that is about 0.4-10x of rented CPUs, depending on the design.
  - The CATCH world has to be in RTL too: the host cannot keep up with about 93k receptor thinnings per life.
  - Break-even, counting 3-6 person-months of development, is about 2-10 million CPU-hours, not 10^4. A whole pilot costs $6-16 on CPUs.
- **What an FPGA is for.** It is not a throughput accelerator at this project's scale. It is useful only as an RTL proving ground for the eventual hardware.
- **Clocklessness:**
  - The tissue needs only local handshakes. But in the simulator the world is a hub that syncs with every sense and act cell at least every d_min.
  - A physical-time clockless ASIC with free-running per-cell oscillators cannot also be deterministic. Exact replay and forks need timestamped logical-time hardware.

**Revised recommendation:** keep option B, the hardware-native integer ABI folded into the ABI-4 cleanup. It is now better supported. Add:
- an integer spec for the world, or keep the world out of the bitwise contract;
- tests of the untested structural changes (walls, FIFO overflow, 32-bit hash);
- the 3-seed evolution A/B.

For speed, use the CPU levers instead: exact fast mode (1.24-1.35x), elastic scheduling and rented cores.
